# Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research

Harish Santhanalakshmi Ganesan Affiliation: Independent researcher
Email: [harishsg99@gmail.com](mailto:)

October 2026

###### Abstract

We present the Infinity Machine, a self-improving AI agent, and use it
for research: problems whose answers can be checked by a program or
against data. It runs three loops. A discovery loop keeps an archive of
scored solutions, and each new candidate is produced by a full
tool-using agent that works for up to an hour in a fresh sandbox,
writing and running its own search code and a lab notebook. A catalogue
mode searches real data for things nobody has catalogued, judged by a
referee rather than a metric. A self-improvement loop lets the system
rewrite its own prompts, tools, skills, memory and meta agent behind a
gate. An autonomous mode chains everything from a single plain-text goal
with no human step: an agent chooses an open problem and writes its
verifier; the kernel calibrates that verifier; an adversarial agent
audits it; the search runs; an agent that never sees the verifier checks
the result; and a final agent writes the report. Proposers see only a
public score; where a task has hidden data (held-out instances, later
observations), a private split that no agent sees decides what counts.
Around this discovery loop the Infinity Machine keeps an editable
_genome_: prompts, tools, skills, an evidence-backed playbook and the
meta agent’s own procedure. A kernel that the agent cannot write to
gates every change to the genome: it checks policy, compares held-in and
held-out performance, and enforces a cost limit. We applied the system
to fourteen problems, thirteen of them external, in six days of October
2026, at a total cost of about \$180 in model usage. It produced four
results beyond the published state of the art on catalogued open
problems in quantum information, each checked by a verifier that the
proposing agent did not write:

- •
  an exactly certified point $`p=0.064966`$ on the positivity ladder of
  the qubit depolarizing channel’s quantum capacity (previous certified
  point $`0.064956`$);
- •
  a single-letter qutrit input that moves that channel’s positivity
  frontier from the hashing value $`0.287087`$ to $`0.2910672`$;
- •
  a 44-gate, depth-6 Clifford circuit preparing the $`[[23,1,7]]`$ Golay
  logical zero, which dominates the published $`(44,8)`$ and $`(45,7)`$;
- •
  an exact ten-term stabilizer decomposition showing
  $`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 7})\leq 10`$ (previously 12).

It also cut the added-gate count of the SABRE qubit-routing benchmark
from SABRE’s 68,559 to 12,087 (9,312 against the best published 13,044
on the 15 circuits shared with later work), built a 5-parameter
transformer that adds 10-digit numbers, closed 24% of the gap between a
20M-parameter language model and the GPT-2 checkpoint on FineWeb
validation loss, and surfaced one unconfirmed planet candidate in TESS
photometry. In hardware, it redesigned the RTL of an open 8$`\times`$8
INT8 systolic matrix-multiply tile. Through a full open RTL-to-GDS flow
at a fixed clock, it cut the energy per multiply-accumulate from
578.9 fJ to 128.8 fJ (77.7% lower) with 55% less area. Power was
measured from gate-level switching activity, and the design stays
bit-exact. In three fully autonomous end-to-end runs (\$7.59–\$9.97
each, no human step after launch), the system chose its problem, wrote
and audited its own verifier, searched, and re-checked its result blind.
One audit rejected a task whose cited record was stale. All three runs
ended in honest ties with the public record, two of them with documented
near misses. In one run the agent-written score pointed the wrong way,
and none of the checks caught it. We report as carefully the parts that
did not work. The system’s one gated attempt to adopt a playbook it had
written for itself was rejected on cost. Proposers gamed lenient
scorers, usually within a single iteration, four times. And the
operator’s hand-made changes to the harness were decisive for several
results. We describe them so the reader can separate what the loop did
from what its operator did.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models can now write and run substantial programs, and
agents built on them can stay on a task for an hour or more. A system
that turns this into discoveries needs two things beyond a capable
model. It must have a way of telling a real advance from a
plausible-looking one, and a way of keeping what it learns.
AlphaEvolve \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] and FunSearch \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] show the
first. They ground an evolutionary search over programs in automatic
evaluation, so that the model’s errors are filtered out by execution,
and they reach new results in mathematics and computer science. Work on
self-improving agents, including STOP \[[3](#bib.bib3)\], the Darwin
Gödel Machine \[[4](#bib.bib4)\], Hyperagents \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] and
AIDE² \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], addresses the second. There the object being
evolved is the agent itself, and recursive
self-improvement \[[7](#bib.bib7)\] is the long-run aim.

The Infinity Machine¹¹ 1 Earlier data deposits call the system EVO; the
two names refer to the same system. is a research agent that does both.
It is not a program-evolution engine with a fixed harness: the unit of
work is a researcher-like agent run, the search can be open-ended as
well as score-driven, and the harness that directs those agents is
itself under gated self-modification. It is built for a single operator
with a laptop and a cloud account. Four design choices define it.

1.  1.  Agents, not samples. A proposal in the Infinity Machine is a full
        agent run. A Deep Agents \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] model with a shell, a
        file system and up to an hour of wall clock in a fresh sandbox reads
        the task notes and the parent solution. It writes and runs its own
        search code and delivers a solution together with a lab notebook. A
        problem therefore receives a handful to about fifteen proposals, not
        thousands. The proposer, not the harness, decides whether to write a
        C tableau simulator, an exhaustive enumeration or a gradient ladder.
2.  2.  A public/private split. Proposers optimise a public score. Where the
        task has hidden data, the result is the score on a private split
        that no agent sees: hidden instances, hidden seeds, or later TESS
        sectors. For exact-verifier tasks the two splits coincide, and the
        “private” score is the same verifier rerun by the kernel in its own
        sandbox. We adopt this split from AIDE² \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]. It
        matters because the agents are strong enough to game any scorer they
        can read
        (Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
3.  3.  The harness is itself an evolvable object. Prompts, tools, skills,
        the playbook and the meta agent’s procedure form a versioned object,
        the genome. A meta agent proposes edits to it, and an immutable
        kernel accepts an edit only if it passes policy, held-in, held-out
        and cost checks
        (Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Self-improvement loop ‣ 2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
4.  4.  End-to-end autonomy with machine-checked trust. The step that
        usually needs a human, deciding that an agent-written evaluator can
        be trusted, is replaced by three machine checks: kernel calibration
        on known cases, an adversarial audit whose exploits the kernel
        replays, and an independent re-check of the final result by an agent
        that never sees the evaluator
        (Section [2.5](#S2.SS5 "2.5 Autonomous mode: from a goal to a verified report ‣ 2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

#### Contributions.

\(i\) The architecture and its kernel/genome split, the discovery loop
with public/private grading, a catalogue mode for open-ended search in
real data, the gated self-improvement loop, and an autonomous mode that
runs from a plain-text goal to a verified report
(Section [2](#S2 "2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
(ii) Results on fourteen problems (thirteen external): four advances on
catalogued open problems in quantum information, a large margin on a
widely used compiler benchmark, two machine-learning tasks and one
astronomy candidate, with every claim checked by a verifier that was not
the agent’s own
(Section [3](#S3 "3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research"),
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
The quantum, SABRE and TESS results are archived with their data and
code on Zenodo (DOIs in the bibliography). (iii) Three fully autonomous
end-to-end runs, whose safeguards caught a stale record before any
search began, and a hardware result: a 77.7% lower energy per MAC for an
open accelerator tile, through a full open chip flow with activity-based
power
(Sections [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
and [3.8](#S3.SS8 "3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
(iv) An account of what the self-improvement machinery did and did not
achieve, of four specification-gaming incidents, and of the operator’s
part in each result
(Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

## 2 The Infinity Machine

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Architecture. The kernel owns everything whose corruption
would make scores meaningless: scorers, private splits, archive, budget
and policy. The genome holds everything the system may change about
itself. Agents run inside sandboxes that mount the genome and the public
split only.

### 2.1 Kernel and genome

The Infinity Machine is split into an immutable _kernel_ and an editable
_genome_
(Figure [1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
The kernel contains a daemon that owns long jobs and survives the
controlling shell, the archive (the genome’s version history as a
lineage DAG, with rollback), the scorers, the gate, the strategy and
model bandits, reward logging, and the budget middleware. The genome
contains the task agent’s and meta agent’s prompts, the meta agent’s
procedure and weakness-mining script, tools with tests, skills with
fixtures, and an ID-addressed playbook in which every bullet carries
evidence run IDs and a confidence. The split follows the rule from
harness-engineering practice \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]: whatever the agent may
legitimately want to change is in the genome, and whatever would let it
change its own grade is not. The kernel never trusts an agent’s report
of what it ran. It records tool calls itself, and scorers read solutions
produced in a fresh sandbox.

### 2.2 Task specification

A task consists of a specification (problem family, description, scorer,
score range and direction, sandbox image and resources, per-run budget,
and a brief), a public split (problem statement, notes, tools, a local
verifier), a private split and an optional seed solution. The scorer is
either a verifier program that the kernel runs in its own sandbox, whose
value is mapped linearly onto $`[0,1]`$, a test suite, or a
retrain-from-code scorer for ML tasks. The brief is the operator’s
channel to the proposers: it lists what has already been measured and
what to try.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: One iteration of the discovery loop. Private scores never
reach an agent. In catalogue mode every proposer extends the shared
merged catalogue instead of a sampled parent, and the referee’s
per-claim verdicts are passed on as feedback.

### 2.3 Discovery loop

A discovery session runs $`N`$ iterations of the loop of
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2.2 Task specification ‣ 2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
with $`P`$ proposers each. The kernel scores the seed and places it in
an _experience bank_. In each iteration it samples $`P`$ parents with
probability proportional to $`\sigma(10\,(s_{\rm pub}-\bar{s}))/(1+c)`$.
Here $`s_{\rm pub}`$ is the parent’s public score, $`\bar{s}`$ is the
mean public score of the top three entries and $`c`$ is the parent’s
number of children. This is the DGM/Hyra rule \[[4](#bib.bib4),
[10](#bib.bib10)\], which favours good parents that have not been
expanded much. Each proposer also receives a named _strategy_, drawn by
a per-family UCB1 bandit whose reward is whether the child beat its
parent on the public score; AIDE² \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] found UCB over
named strategies to be its most valuable discovered mechanism. The
default arms, written for the optimisation family and used by every
family without its own set, are _conservative_, _aggressive rewrite_,
_new neighbourhood_, _data structure_ and _robust/simple_. Math tasks
use _structured construction_, _exhaustive small case_, _new objective_,
_scale compute_ and _literature transfer_. ML tasks use _new
architecture family_, _parameter sharing_, _embedding budget_,
_connectivity_ and _recipe_; astronomy tasks have five search-oriented
arms of their own.

A proposer is a fresh Deep Agents model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) in a sandbox
that mounts the genome, the task’s public split and an inspiration
folder: the parent solution and a bank summary that shows public scores
only. It works with a shell for up to about an hour. It must keep its
solution directory current, because a per-run spend cap (\$4 by
default), checked before every model call, can end it at any turn. On
return, the kernel scores the solution on both splits in a separate
sandbox, appends it to the bank and logs the strategy reward. The
session’s answer is the best _public_ solution, and its _private_ score
is what we report.

#### Catalogue mode.

Optimisation has a parent to improve; open-ended discovery in real data
does not. A task in catalogue mode changes the deliverable to a list of
claims plus a search log. The scorer becomes a _referee_, which
re-measures every claim from the raw data, checks it against catalogues
of known objects and returns per-claim verdicts. Those verdicts reach
the next proposer as feedback. The hidden split is _prediction_: for the
TESS task, the private verifier mounts later observing sectors that no
agent can read and checks whether each periodic claim predicts dips
there. After each round the kernel merges all accepted claims into one
shared catalogue, which every proposer then extends.

### 2.4 Self-improvement loop

The self-improvement loop improves the genome rather than a solution. A
UCB or score-child selector picks a parent generation. The meta agent
(Claude Opus 5.5), whose prompt and procedure are themselves genome
files \[[5](#bib.bib5)\], reads an evidence bundle of recent runs and
mines weaknesses. It proposes one bounded edit together with a manifest
that states the evidence, the root cause and the predicted fixes. The
kernel then applies a static policy check (only genome paths may change,
kernel-owned files are byte-identical, at most 12 files) and grades the
candidate on held-in and held-out tasks. It accepts the candidate only
if neither split regresses beyond a noise band of 0.03 and the cost is
at most 1.5 times the incumbent’s. A gain larger than 0.3 is parked for
human review instead of being activated. Predictions in the manifest are
checked against per-task deltas, and a meta agent whose predictions keep
failing is sampled less often.

Three further paths feed the genome.
*Consolidation* \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] reflects on run records and edits
playbook bullets by ID. Bullets that a run retrieved are confirmed or
weakened by that run’s outcome, and recurring lessons are promoted to
skills, which must pass a fixture. _Capability requests_ let a task
agent ask for a tool; a toolsmith subagent writes it with tests, and the
kernel re-runs those tests before the requester may use the tool.
_Rewards_ come from scores and from the operator’s good/bad feedback on
individual runs, and update the bandits and playbook confidence. Every
path ends in a generation that passes the same gate, so every
self-modification is auditable and reversible.

### 2.5 Autonomous mode: from a goal to a verified report

In the modes above a human writes the task: the problem statement, the
verifier, the seed and the notes. Autonomous mode removes that step. Its
only input is a plain-text research goal; the default goal asks for an
open problem whose best known result is an explicit object or number
that a program can check exactly. Every phase is an agent run in its own
fresh sandbox, and the kernel only validates, routes and records
(Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.5 Autonomous mode: from a goal to a verified report ‣ 2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

1.  1.  Scout (network on). The scout surveys public problem catalogues and
        the literature, picks one problem, and checks that it is still open.
        It writes a complete task to a fixed contract: a task specification
        with the record and its source, a problem statement, a verifier
        program, a seed solution, at least four calibration cases with known
        outcomes (valid ones with their exact values, invalid ones that must
        be rejected), and a selection note with the evidence of openness.
2.  2.  Kernel validation. The kernel runs the verifier on the seed and on
        every calibration case in a network-off sandbox. Valid cases must
        reproduce their stated values, and invalid cases must be rejected or
        score no better than the seed. The scoring range must also extend
        beyond the record, so that beating the record registers.
3.  3.  Adversarial audit (network on). A fresh agent re-checks that the
        problem is open and the record current, and tries to construct
        invalid solutions that the verifier accepts at or above the record.
        The kernel replays every exploit file through the verifier. The
        audit fails if the auditor says so or if any exploit is accepted.
        Its findings go back to the scout for a repair round (at most three
        rounds).
4.  4.  Installation. The task is installed and the approval is recorded as
        automatic, with its basis (calibration, audit and exploit replay).
        This replaces the human approval that an agent-proposed evaluator
        otherwise requires.
5.  5.  Discovery. The ordinary loop of
        Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Discovery loop ‣ 2 The Infinity Machine ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
        runs on the generated task.
6.  6.  Independent check (network off). A fresh agent receives only the
        problem statement and the best solution, never the verifier. It
        writes its own checker, tests it on cases it constructs, and
        evaluates the solution. The kernel compares the two values.
7.  7.  Report. A fresh agent writes a report and a machine-readable claim:
        the problem, the record and its source, the result, how it was
        verified, and an explicit claim boundary.

The protocol is generic: the briefs contain no problem-specific
knowledge. All artefacts and events are kept under the session’s run
directory for audit.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Autonomous mode. Grey: agent runs, each in a fresh sandbox.
Blue: kernel steps. Nothing between the goal and the report requires a
human.

### 2.6 Infrastructure and the operator

Sandboxes are local Docker containers (network off, read-only root, no
kernel files, no private split) or Modal sandboxes behind the same
interface. Modal provides GPU (one H100) and read-only data volumes for
the ML and astronomy tasks. A daemon owns sessions, so a closed terminal
does not kill a run, provided the session is submitted as a daemon job;
one session started from a foreground shell lost a proposer run when
that shell died
(Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

The fourteen problem campaigns of
Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Quantum capacity thresholds ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")–[3.7](#S3.SS7 "3.7 Null results ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
were run before autonomous mode existed, and in them the operator’s role
was substantial. The accelerator campaign
(Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research"))
ran later, in the same operator-led way. We want to be exact about it.
For each of those problems the operator, working with an AI coding
assistant:

- •
  chose and vetted the problem against the literature;
- •
  wrote the verifier, seed and task notes;
- •
  launched the sessions;
- •
  gave run-level feedback;
- •
  after each session, updated the notes with an “already measured”
  table, which was the main channel by which one session learned from
  the last;
- •
  fixed kernel bugs;
- •
  re-verified and certified every result on the host, and wrote and
  deposited the notes.

The operator also wrote family-specific strategy arms by hand three
times (math and ML after observing failures, and astronomy when adding
catalogue mode). Under our own rules that is a kernel change rather than
a genome change, but it shaped later results, and we discuss it in
Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research").
In the three autonomous runs
(Section [3.8](#S3.SS8 "3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research"))
the operator’s only actions were writing the goal text and launching the
job: an agent chose the problem and wrote the task, and the kernel and
other agents did everything up to and including the report.
