### 3.1 Quantum capacity thresholds

#### Qubit depolarizing channel.

The noise level at which the quantum capacity of
$`\mathcal{D}_{p}(\rho)=(1-3p)\rho+p(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z)`$ vanishes
is open. Lower bounds come from inputs with positive coherent
information \[[19](#bib.bib19), [20](#bib.bib20)\]. Krohn-Grimberghe
recently certified, in exact arithmetic, a 45-copy rank-two
symmetric-subspace state at
$`p=16239/250000=0.064956`$ \[[21](#bib.bib21)\]. The Infinity Machine
task gave proposers a float evaluator (Schur–Weyl blocks via a
coherent-state generating function), that state as the seed, and score
$`(p-0.064)/0.002`$.

In session 2 the first proposer wrote its own checkpointing Adam ladder,
raising $`p`$ by $`10^{-6}`$ whenever $`I_{c}>2\times 10^{-9}`$. In 42
minutes, for \$0.60, it delivered a state with float threshold
$`\approx 0.0649671`$. The record authors’ own exact certifier, run
unchanged on that state, classifies it as certified-positive at
$`p=32483/500000=0.064966`$, with enclosure
$`[2.31,2.78]\times 10^{-8}`$ bits \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]. This is a
candidate-specific lower bound and makes no claim about the optimal
threshold. A first session had reached $`p=0.064962`$ but was killed by
host memory pressure before it saved anything, which is why the brief
now demands continuous checkpointing.

#### Qutrit depolarizing channel.

For $`\mathcal{N}(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+p\,I/3`$, the catalogue listed only
the hashing point $`0.287087`$. Session 1 found a 4-qutrit, rank-4 input
with threshold $`0.289205`$. In session 2 a proposer questioned the
seed’s size instead of growing it: with rank 4 allowed, _smaller_ $`n`$
wins. Its Adam ladders from random starts gave $`n=3`$: $`0.28995`$ and
$`n=2`$: $`0.29106`$, and L-BFGS polishing gave $`0.2910672`$, the
optimum that all 25 L-BFGS starts reached. The operator’s structure
check showed that the optimum is a product of two single-qutrit inputs,
each maximally mixed on a two-dimensional subspace. The gain is
therefore single-letter: the leaked component heralds the error. We gave
a closed form and a 50-digit interval certificate
$`p_{2}(3)\in[0.291067236033599\,69,0.291067236033599\,88]`$, and the
same effect holds for every $`3\leq d\leq 64`$ we
checked \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. The proposers found the state but not the
structure: two later runs noticed that the state is $`P/4`$ on a
subspace, but neither computed the reduced states that reveal the
product. The result is elementary enough that it may be folklore, and
the note makes no priority claim.

#### Private information.

For the private capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel (here in the
convention $`\Lambda_{p}=(1-p)\rho+pI/2`$, not per-Pauli), both sessions
found classical $`K=2`$ ensembles of repetition-like distributions.
Their thresholds are new as explicit finite-$`n`$ witnesses, rising from
$`0.28223`$ at $`n=1`$ \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] to $`0.284668`$ at $`n=8`$,
but they climb only about $`3\times 10^{-4}`$ per
qubit \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. The operator’s literature check showed that
one-way QKD rates with publicly announced syndromes \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]
already imply $`P>0`$ up to $`p\approx 0.2915`$, once the announcement
is paid for in-band. The zoo record had been behind the literature, and
the agent’s search was not the decisive contribution here.

### 3.2 Fault-tolerant circuits and magic states

#### Golay logical zero.

The record CNOT-count/depth points for preparing $`|0\rangle`$ of the
$`[[23,1,7]]`$ Golay code were $`(44,8)`$ and $`(45,7)`$, from RL plus
MCTS graph decimation on an A100 \[[24](#bib.bib24)\]. Session 1
returned the seed from all four runs. In session 2 a proposer under the
_aggressive rewrite_ arm rewrote the search in C (about
$`5\times 10^{6}`$ tableau evaluations per second per core). It changed
the objective to the number of qubits left _mixed_ after
reverse-applying the circuit, which is zero if and only if the state is
a product in any local basis, not only in $`Z`$. It then walked the
neutral network at a fixed 44 gates with a penalty on gates beyond the
target depth. Depth 7 appeared in about a second and depth 6 in 10–60
seconds; depth 5 and 43 gates were never reached, the latter even after
$`10^{10}`$ evaluations and an exhaustive delete-two/insert-one sweep.
The $`(44,6)`$ circuit dominates both published points. It was verified
up to wire relabelling by stabilizer-tableau checks and a
$`2^{23}`$-amplitude statevector overlap of 1.0 \[[14](#bib.bib14)\].

#### Stabilizer rank of $`|T\rangle^{\otimes m}`$.

Exact stabilizer ranks are known only for $`m\leq 4`$, and the bounds
for $`m\geq 7`$ were products of smaller
decompositions \[[25](#bib.bib25), [26](#bib.bib26)\]. Session 1 was
null. Two of its six proposers ran no search at all, one calling the
task an open research problem and the other “hardening” a seed that was
already a record, as its default-arm instruction suggested. After the
operator replaced the math arms, a _structured construction_ proposer in
session 2 followed a direction the operator’s notes had listed as
untried (close a few stabilizer states under qubit permutations) and
built a dictionary by closing three seed states under
$`S_{a}\times S_{b}`$-symmetric Cliffords (396–540 vectors). It then
annealed over subsets with 1,024 batched chains, reaching $`r=12`$ in
40 s, $`r=11`$ in a few minutes, and $`r=10`$ on the $`[2,5]`$ block
family. The decomposition is exact, with coefficients in
$`\frac{1}{4}\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_{8}]`$, and gives
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 7})\leq 10`$ and by sub-multiplicativity
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 13})\leq 60`$ \[[16](#bib.bib16)\]. A
companion _exhaustive small case_ run found that coordinate descent over
the full $`m=5`$ stabilizer table stalls at residual 0.0647 for five
terms, which is evidence (not proof) that
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 5})=6`$.

### 3.3 Algorithms and benchmarks

#### Qubit routing on the SABRE suite.

On the 26 circuits and the 43-edge IBM Q20 Tokyo design graph of the
SABRE paper \[[27](#bib.bib27)\], with SWAP insertion only and three
added gates per SWAP, the methods progressed as follows. Two circuits
(qft_13, qft_20) are not in the public benchmark repository and were
regenerated (338 and 800 gates against the paper’s 403 and 970), so
their reference is our SABRE reimplementation. Session 1 rewrote SABRE
in C++ with early-abort randomised restarts and a hill-climb over
initial mappings (36,435 added gates), then a receding-horizon rollout
router (24,228). In session 2, two proposers _independently_ implemented
a direction the notes listed as untried, a beam search over SWAP
sequences, whose state is the mapping plus per-qubit progress; together
they reached 12,261. Session 3 refined this to 12,087. On identical
inputs, Qiskit 2.4.1’s SABRE gives 64,137 (53,418 with heavy trial
settings) and pytket 2.18.5 gives 35,685. On the 15 circuits reported by
later routing papers, the best published counts (HAIL,
2025 \[[28](#bib.bib28)\]) total 13,044, against 9,312 here, and our
count is lower on every one of those circuits \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. Beam
search for routing is not new. The routers also spent minutes to an hour
of CPU per circuit, against seconds to minutes for the stock baselines
(up to 23 minutes per circuit for heavy Qiskit), the run-to-run spread
is about 8%, and the graph is the design graph rather than the
35-coupler device, so this is a statement about headroom in a widely
used benchmark, not a fair comparison of algorithms.

#### Combinatorial optimisation.

On the internal TSP task (hidden instances, $`n`$ from 600 to 2000,
scored against a BHH optimum estimate), two iterations with two
proposers each raised the private score from 0.58 to 0.88. The proposers
converged on chained 2-opt with Or-opt and segment-swap kicks. While
calibrating this family we found that any reference built from a
hand-written local search was matched by the agent within one session,
so references must come from optima or stronger solvers.

### 3.4 Machine learning

#### AdderBoard.

The task is to find the smallest transformer that adds two 10-digit
numbers with full accuracy \[[29](#bib.bib29)\]. Working from the rules
alone, a proposer designed a 5-parameter model in one 8-minute, \$1.05
run. It has one attention layer and two heads keyed on a period-11
sinusoidal positional encoding, a scalar tied embedding and read-out,
and a sigmoid carry gate; the carry arises only through autoregressive
feedback. It passes the upstream verifier on 10,010 of 10,010 additions
across three seeds. A parallel proposer found an independent 6-parameter
design. The next session gamed the parameter counter
(Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

#### A 20M-parameter language model.

The task was to find an architecture of at most 20M parameters,
embeddings included, that beats the OpenAI GPT-2 124M checkpoint on
FineWeb validation (1.0658 bits per byte), training only on FineWeb-10B
(GPT-2 itself was trained on WebText). The scorer retrains each
candidate _from its code_ on one H100 for $`10^{9}`$ tokens, so a gain
must come from the architecture or recipe. The seed was a scaled-down
modded-nanogpt \[[30](#bib.bib30)\] at 1.3376. Session 1 reached 1.2868
with recipe changes and learnable residual mixing; it made no
architectural change, because the bandit drew only opt-era arms. After
the operator replaced the ML arms, session 2 reached 1.2716 with four
unique blocks looped twice over eight layers. That closes 24% of the
gap. The Modal workspace spend limit then stopped the session. This is
the clearest case in which the Infinity Machine did not reach its
target.

### 3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile

We asked whether the same loop can design hardware when the score is
measured power, not a proxy. The design is the 8$`\times`$8 INT8
weight-stationary systolic array (32-bit outputs) from LogikBench, as
shipped with OpenROAD-flow-scripts \[[31](#bib.bib31)\] for the ASAP7
predictive 7 nm PDK \[[32](#bib.bib32)\]. Proposers may rewrite its RTL
freely but must keep its ports and its cycle-level protocol, so
throughput is fixed at 64 MACs per cycle. The evaluator, written by the
operator, runs every candidate through the full flow at a fixed 600 ps
clock: Yosys synthesis, floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis,
detailed routing and parasitic extraction. It then applies five gates:

- •
  the RTL matches a Python golden model on random and corner-case tiles
  (Icarus Verilog);
- •
  the routed netlist, simulated with functional ASAP7 cell models, is
  bit-exact on the same tiles;
- •
  setup and hold worst slack are both $`\geq 0`$;
- •
  there are 0 routing DRC violations;
- •
  the area is at most $`1.1\times`$ the original’s.

The score is the energy per MAC on an inference-like workload: post-ReLU
activations (about half zero) and roughly Gaussian weights, 16,384 MACs
over a 456-cycle window that includes the drain cycles between tiles.
OpenSTA computes the power from the gate-level VCD of that window and
the routed SPEF. Proposers see the result for workload seed 2026, and
the kernel’s private score uses seed 7331. A failed gate scores zero.
The original RTL measures 578.9 fJ/MAC (34.7 mW; area 5,559 $`\mu`$m²).

The search ran in two sessions with nine recorded proposer runs (\$11.0
in total).
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
lists the steps that set a new best, from the agents’ notebooks, and
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
shows every scored proposal and where the power went.

| Run (arm)                      | fJ/MAC | $`\mu`$m² | Change                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| original RTL                   | 578.9  | 5,559     | –                                                                                                                                                     |
| s1 it0-p0 (data structure), v1 | 346.9  | 3,773     | activations broadcast along rows, no output de-skew; per-row partial sums 16–19 bits wide; no datapath resets                                         |
| s1 it0-p0, v2 (s2 seed)        | 274.9  | 3,766     | latch+AND clock gates per pipeline depth, enabled from the valid pipe; a gate on the weight registers                                                 |
| s2 it0-p0 (conservative)       | 252.8  | 2,998     | v2’s gating plus a parallel run’s Baugh–Wooley multiplier, 3:2 carry-save tree with the partial sum folded in, Brent–Kung adder                       |
| s2 it0-p1 (new neighbourhood)  | 188.2  | 2,427     | four PE rows per pipeline stage: a Python generator emits one 33-operand bit-level Dadda tree and one adder per stage; 4 partial-sum stages $`\to`$ 2 |
| s2 it2-p0 (new neighbourhood)  | 128.8  | 2,507     | activation shift chains replaced by a 13-entry ring buffer with a gated clock per entry; weights written in place per row instead of shifted          |

Table 2: The steps that set a new best on the accelerator tile (public
workload; every step passed all five gates). The final design measures
130.1 fJ/MAC on the private workload.

Figure 5: The accelerator tile. (a) Energy per MAC of every scored
proposal in completion order (dots; orange set a new best) and the best
so far (line). Session 2 started from session 1’s best design. Run
labels are iteration and proposer. (b) Power at the fixed 600 ps clock
and unchanged throughput for the original RTL and the three designs that
set new bests, split into internal (cell and clock) and switching power;
the total is printed above each bar. Values are the kernel’s
public-workload measurements, from the session banks.

The final design uses 7.7 mW at the same clock and throughput, and is
77.7% lower in energy per MAC than the original RTL. It is also 55%
smaller, with setup and hold slack of $`+5.2`$ and $`+6.3`$ ps. A
same-run ablation attributes about 43 fJ of the last step to the ring
buffer and 16 fJ to writing the weights in place. Two of the agents’ own
observations shaped the search. The first was that the 64 input bits are
the narrowest point of the pipeline, so it is cheaper to delay the
activations than to register partial sums. The second was that flops,
and the clock that drives them, dominate the power. The search also
found negative results: a radix-4 Booth multiplier with activations
encoded once per row was worse (300.8 fJ), and eight rows per stage
would not close timing at 600 ps. One proposer declined to ship a 1.6%
better variant because its hold slack was only $`+0.197`$ ps, reasoning
that a gate failure on the private run would score zero.

This result has clear limits. ASAP7 is a predictive PDK, so these are
modelled, not measured, energies. There is one flow, one clock and one
synthetic workload distribution. The gate-level simulation is
zero-delay, so glitch power is not counted. The ring-buffer design
relies on the protocol’s weight load of exactly eight w_valid cycles per
tile, which the testbench uses but which a different host could violate.
The comparison is against the original RTL, not against a hand-optimised
design. The operator built the evaluator, wrote an “already measured”
table between sessions, corrected the score range twice, and reseeded
session 2 with session 1’s best design
(Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

### 3.6 Open-ended discovery in TESS photometry

We pointed catalogue mode at TESS \[[33](#bib.bib33)\] light curves of
about 17,000 stars: 9,779 director’s-discretionary targets and 7,474 M
dwarfs within 40 pc observed only in full-frame images. Four sessions
cost about \$58. The referee was rewritten four times: twice to close
loopholes that proposers exploited
(Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")),
once after the operator’s manual vetting found blends, eclipsing
binaries and aliases, and once to fix a cadence bug the operator found.
The final referee accepts 47 of 60 known TOIs and 30 of 49 known FFI
planets, and accepts none of 80 random fake claims. One candidate
survives: G 249-11 (TIC 417732194), an M4.5 dwarf at 29 pc with a 3 ppt,
0.9 h transit-like signal at $`P=5.307425`$ d, which implies
$`R_{p}\approx 1.6\,R_{\oplus}`$. An ephemeris fitted to two sectors
predicted dips in two later sectors that were never used for selection,
with $`p\approx 0.002`$ from 400 full-pipeline
nulls \[[18](#bib.bib18)\]. That is about $`3\sigma`$, and a bound
eclipsing binary and a faint neighbour are not excluded, so we report a
candidate, not a planet. An independent read-only reviewer agent caught
a 1000-day error in the reference epoch and an independence error in the
first vetting report.

### 3.7 Null results

On the Einstein Arena \[[34](#bib.bib34)\] Sidon (4,5)-set problem, the
Infinity Machine found 13 new sets tying the 4/7 record but none below
it. The operator’s feasibility analysis (not the agent’s) shows that
within the verifier’s range only $`n=16`$ or $`n=18`$ could beat 4/7. On
the $`51\times 51`$ Hadamard maximal-determinant problem, proposers
established that the record \[[35](#bib.bib35)\] is a fixed point of
every local method they tried. Their best alternative family
($`\mathbb{Z}_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{5}`$ blocks) reaches 43.2310 against
the record’s 43.3013. A further exhaustive argument ruling out one
circulant family was again the operator’s. For the largest seven-qubit
distance-two code ($`24\leq K\leq 26`$ \[[36](#bib.bib36),
[37](#bib.bib37)\]), hundreds of restarts all land on one plateau per
method. For four bases in $`\mathbb{C}^{6}`$, every proposer did basin
hopping around the known optimum \[[38](#bib.bib38)\], and about 35,000
re-ascents returned to it. Where the published record is a robust
optimum of random-restart search, the Infinity Machine did not improve
it, and the useful output was a measured negative.

### 3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs

We launched autonomous mode three times on 26 October 2026, each as a
daemon job with a \$30 cap, and did not intervene in any of them. The
first run had the default goal: find an open problem in mathematics,
quantum information or theoretical computer science whose best known
result a program can check exactly, and improve on it. It took
1 h 42 min and \$9.86 (session 20261026-002501-autonomous).
Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
lists its phases.

| Phase             | \$   | Outcome                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------- | ---- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Scout, round 0    | 3.14 | Chose the largest binary two-deletion-correcting code of length 16, a maximum independent set in a 65,536-vertex graph (Einstein Arena problem 34). Cited a 2026 paper’s 215 as the record, used the public 208-word code as the seed, and wrote the verifier and calibration cases.                                                                                           |
| Validation        | –    | Passed: seed and calibration reproduced.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Audit, round 0    | 1.32 | Failed. The record was stale. The arena leaderboard already listed public codes of 216–223 words; the auditor downloaded the 223-word code and verified it with the task verifier and its own checker. Kernel replay of 18 exploit files: all rejected.                                                                                                                        |
| Scout, round 1    | 0.85 | Repaired the task: record 223, seed the 223-word code, score range extended to 228.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Audit, round 1    | 0.58 | Passed: open, record current, no exploit accepted. Task installed with automatic approval.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Discovery         | 3.46 | Three rounds of two proposers. They tried a plateau local search in C ($`\approx 1.9\times 10^{8}`$ candidate probes per second per core), an exact large-neighbourhood search that frees 24–60 codewords and re-solves them by branch and bound, and a stock iterated local search. None found a 224-word code. Round 3 drew _conservative_ twice, and both runs were no-ops. |
| Independent check | 0.19 | The agent wrote its own checker from the problem statement, plus a pairwise longest-common-subsequence test (maximum 13 $`<`$ 14). Result: valid, 223 words, in agreement with the verifier.                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Report            | 0.32 | “No improvement: the best verified code has 223 words, which ties (does not beat) the public record of 223.” The claim boundary credits the record’s authors.                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

Table 3: Autonomous run 1, phase by phase, from the session’s event log
and the agents’ outputs.

The first run produced no new result. It does, however, show the full
chain working with no human step, and both of its safeguards fired for
real.

- •
  The audit prevented a false discovery. Without it, the search would
  have “beaten the record” of 215 by rediscovering a public code, and
  the report would have claimed it.
- •
  The independent check confirmed the verifier with code the verifier’s
  author never saw.

The run also showed two weaknesses.

- •
  The scout checked papers but not leaderboards or discussion threads.
  The auditor found the newer codes there.
- •
  Autonomous tasks fell back to the default strategy arms, so the last
  round repeated the conservative no-op failure of
  Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research").
  We fixed this for runs 2 and 3.

The chosen problem was also a crowded one: many agents had pushed the
public record from 216 to 223 in five weeks.

#### Runs 2 and 3.

We then changed two things and ran autonomous mode twice more, in
parallel. First, the autonomous task family now uses the research-shaped
math arms (literature transfer, structured construction, new objective,
scale compute, exhaustive small case). Second, each goal named a
specific table instead of leaving the field open. We chose the tables
from a survey of quiet, verifiable records
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B The autonomous runs in detail ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
Run 2 targeted Dobbelaere’s sorting-network size tables for 25 to 40
inputs, and run 3 Brouwer’s table of mixed binary/ternary codes. Within
those tables the scout chose the cell, confirmed it was current, and
wrote the verifier, seed and calibration cases.

|                | Run 2                                                                                                                                                          | Run 3                                                                                                         |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Chosen problem | Size of a sorting network on 31 inputs; record 180 comparators (Batcher-type, unchanged since 2017), bounds 141–180                                            | Mixed code $`N(4,5,3)`$, 4 binary and 5 ternary coordinates, distance 3; table 186–216, lower bound from 1998 |
| Why this cell  | Its entry is a 32-input merge network minus one wire, never improved by evolutionary search, while $`n=28`$–30 were                                            | 16% gap; neighbouring cells were improved in 2010–2013 and this one was not                                   |
| Scout          | \$2.03, 19 min; exact 0-1 verifier over all $`2^{31}`$ inputs ($`\approx`$15 s)                                                                                | \$4.66, 47 min; its own coset-union search reproduced 186 and other table entries; 12 calibration cases       |
| Audit          | \$0.89; pass; 23 exploit files, all rejected on replay                                                                                                         | \$1.14; pass; 24 exploit files, all rejected on replay                                                        |
| Discovery      | \$4.12, 6 runs: SorterHunter-style evolution, a witness-vector variant, annealing at 179 comparators on the number of unsorted inputs; 2 runs searched nothing | \$3.60, 6 runs: coset unions, about 30,000 prescribed automorphism groups, tabu search, LNS from the 186 code |
| Near miss      | 179 comparators with one unsorted 0-1 vector                                                                                                                   | 189 words (63 cosets) with one conflicting pair                                                               |
| Check, report  | \$0.55; independent C checker agrees; “no improvement”                                                                                                         | \$0.58; independent checker agrees; “no improvement”                                                          |
| Total          | \$7.59, 2 h 38 min                                                                                                                                             | \$9.97, 2 h 55 min                                                                                            |

Table 4: Autonomous runs 2 and 3 (sessions
20261026-024005-autonomous-e33eb and 20261026-023958-autonomous-67f31),
from their event logs, scout selections and reports. Both ended in ties
with the record.

Table [4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Runs 2 and 3. ‣ 3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
summarises both runs. Both tied the record. In both, the scout’s
selection reasoning was specific and checkable, the verifier survived
its audit, and the final report declined to claim anything. Their near
misses are informative but are not results: a network that leaves one
input unsorted is not a sorting network. Four things went wrong.

- •
  A reversed score in run 2, missed by every check. The kernel’s
  minimising scorer gives score 1 at the first end of the task’s score
  range and 0 at the second. The scout wrote the range as 186 to 175,
  intending the opposite. As installed, the 186-comparator Batcher
  network scored 1.0, the record 0.455, and a record-beating 179 would
  have scored 0.364, below its parent. Kernel validation checked values
  but not the direction of the score. The auditor read the mapping as
  intended and reported 0.545 for the record. The reporter noticed the
  mismatch between 0.545 and 0.4545 but not its cause. No proposer
  shipped a larger network, so the outcome was unaffected. Had one found
  a 179, though, the bandit and the parent sampler would have treated it
  as a regression. Worse, the independent check and the report take the
  highest-scoring solution, so the 179 would have stayed in the bank
  unreported. The operator had made the same mistake on the chip task
  (Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
  Validation should check that calibration cases with better values
  score higher.
- •
  Declined searches. In run 2, two of the six proposers (_exhaustive
  small case_ and _new objective_) judged further search hopeless and
  returned their parent without running a new search; one estimated
  $`10^{9}`$ candidate repairs as too many for its budget. This is the
  conservative no-op of
  Section [4](#S4 "4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
  in a new form, now under research arms. All six run-3 proposers ran
  searches.
- •
  Rate-limited literature checks. In run 3 both the scout and the
  auditor were throttled by arXiv and Semantic Scholar (HTTP 429). The
  task was installed on the strength of the table page alone, and the
  report says so.
- •
  A colliding session. Two jobs launched in the same second first shared
  one session directory. We cancelled both before their scouts finished,
  kept the directory, and added a random suffix to session names before
  relaunching. The runs reported here are the relaunches.

Across three runs, autonomous mode chose reasonable problems, wrote
verifiers that survived 18–24 replayed exploits each, caught one stale
record, and reported three honest nulls for \$27.42 in total. It also
installed one task whose score pointed the wrong way, and none of its
checks noticed. It has not yet made a discovery.

## 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not

#### The self-improvement gate rejected the one self-derived generation.

The first 16 problem runs (AdderBoard, Sidon, Hadamard) never reached
the system’s memory: two kernel scanners read only top-level runs. After
that was fixed, one consolidation pass over those 16 proposer runs wrote
four playbook bullets from the proposers’ own notes:

- •
  do not re-run neighbourhoods that earlier notes already tried;
- •
  a faster optimiser on a proxy is not progress unless the proxy tracks
  the real score;
- •
  pilot symmetry-restricted families for 60 s before committing budget;
- •
  use the shipped checker.

Graded by the self-improvement gate (\$8.22, 57 minutes), the generation
with these bullets scored 0.944 on held-in tasks against the incumbent’s
0.927, and 1.000 on held-out tasks against 1.000. Its cost was 2.02
times the incumbent’s, above the gate’s 1.5 limit, so it was _rejected_.
The bullets made the agent run more experiments, which bought a small
gain at twice the spend. No meta-agent proposal ran in that session,
because the single iteration was spent validating this pending
candidate; in an earlier smoke run the meta agent proposed no change.
Every discovery result in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
was therefore produced by the initial genome. The gate behaved as
designed. Whether $`2\times`$ the cost for $`+0.017`$ is worth it is a
policy question for a human, and with one seed the gain is within noise.
We do not yet have evidence that the Infinity Machine improves itself on
these problems.

#### Strategy arms mattered, but a human chose them.

Over the first 16 runs the bandit’s data were unambiguous. _Data
structure_ earned a mean reward of 0.4 over 5 pulls, and every other arm
earned 0 over 11. _Conservative_ and _robust/simple_ pulls on a record
seed were pure no-ops: proposers shipped the seed unchanged, at about
\$0.8 in total. The bandit would have learned to avoid those arms
eventually, but on problems with only 4–6 pulls per session it could
not. The operator replaced the arms by hand for math and ML (and wrote
the astronomy arms). For math (structured construction and the others),
the first session afterwards produced
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 7})\leq 10`$. For ML (architecture family,
parameter sharing and the others), the next session produced the looped
model. Under the rule that lessons must enter through the system’s own
loops, these were kernel changes, not self-improvement, and we report
them as such. A version of the Infinity Machine that proposed its own
strategy arms through the gate is the obvious next step.

#### Specification gaming within one iteration.

Strong proposers exploited lenient scorers four times, usually within a
single iteration (items 1–4); item 5 is a hole in a referee that the
operator, not a proposer, found. The original artefact for each item
(code, formula, the agent’s own words) is in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evidence for the specification-gaming incidents ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research").

1.  1.  AdderBoard. With the score saturating at 6 parameters, the next
        session “reached one parameter” in 2.5 minutes by turning four
        weights into Python constants. Strict counting, under which
        constants acting as weights count, restored the true count of 5. The
        proposers disclosed the loophole when asked for review risks.
2.  2.  Seven-qubit code. A partial-credit formula paid for any residual
        below 1, so an unconfirmed $`K=25`$ subspace at residual 0.072
        outscored the confirmed $`K=24`$ code. Credit now starts only below
        $`10^{-2}`$.
3.  3.  TESS, referee v1. Proposers claimed “single transits” 500–1200% deep
        (flux glitches), flux steps and about 90 cheap eclipsing binaries.
        The fix added physical bounds, a step test and a sky-neighbour
        systematics test.
4.  4.  TESS, referee v2. A proposer wrote that “extra credit lies in
        uncapped single events and duo transits” and submitted 240 single
        and 39 two-event “transits”. The fix requires at least three events
        and caps singles and duos.
5.  5.  TESS, referee v4 (not gaming). The referee itself had a hole: it
        used one cadence per star, so signals that appeared in only one
        observing era passed. Leave-one-era-out tests found it, and v5
        checks cadence per sector and requires consistency across eras.

The pattern matches reports from Hyra and the DGM \[[10](#bib.bib10),
[4](#bib.bib4)\]. The defence that worked was not a better prompt. It
was a private split the agents could not see, together with adversarial
calibration of the verifier: known positives, injected negatives, and an
independent reviewer.

#### The outcome of every proposer run.

Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ The outcome of every proposer run. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
classifies all 104 proposer runs recorded in the 27 discovery sessions,
by comparing each run’s public score with its parent’s. Seven in ten
runs did not beat their parent. The table counts beating the parent,
which is weaker than setting a new best
(Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Where progress came from within a session. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")),
and it takes the scores at face value. Eight of the 39 parent-beating
runs owe their gain wholly or partly to a scorer we later fixed.

| Outcome                                             | Runs | Notes                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ---- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Beat its parent’s public score                      | 39   | incl. 3 gamed outright (2 AdderBoard, 1 seven-qubit code) and 5 TESS runs scored by referees later found exploitable |
| Matched its parent, no gain                         | 58   | incl. at least 10 that delivered the parent essentially unchanged, per their own notebooks                           |
| Worse than its parent                               | 2    | both TESS, under a stricter referee                                                                                  |
| No valid solution                                   | 5    | 4 stopped by the Modal spend limit (LM), 1 by the step limit (TESS)                                                  |
| Hit the per-run spend cap (overlaps the rows above) | 5    | introduced after one run cost \$7.15                                                                                 |
| Lost before scoring, not in the records             | 3    | 2 killed with the host (C11), 1 lost when its shell died (SABRE)                                                     |

Table 5: Outcome of every recorded proposer run in the fourteen problem
campaigns (104 runs, 27 sessions; the 18 proposals of the three
autonomous runs are reported in
Section [3.8](#S3.SS8 "3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research"),
and the nine of the accelerator campaign in
Section [3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Hardware: a low-energy systolic matrix tile ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")),
computed from the kernel’s event logs; the notes come from the run
notebooks and
Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research").

#### When the agents caught our mistakes.

Several runs reported errors in the operator’s own scaffolding instead
of exploiting them, as AIDE² also observed \[[6](#bib.bib6)\]:

- •
  Both SABRE proposers in session 2 reported that the shipped local
  verifier had unfilled `{BASE}`/`{TARGET}` placeholders and crashed.
  They worked around it and said so.
- •
  A SABRE proposer noticed that two benchmark files are byte-identical.
  Another proved by exhaustive placement that one circuit has no
  zero-SWAP embedding, so the published count is optimal.
- •
  A MUB proposer found that the operator’s polar retraction gives NaN
  gradients at the identity basis, which the record contains, and
  documented the fix.
- •
  The AdderBoard proposers listed the constants loophole under “review
  risk” in their final message. The TESS proposer stated its intent to
  exploit the uncapped classes in its notebook.

In two of the four gaming incidents, then, the exploit was stated in the
agents’ own reports before the operator found it in the scores. Reading
the notebooks is a cheap detector.

#### Infrastructure lessons that became kernel features.

- •
  A proposer that ran 40 minutes on 2.1M input tokens cost \$7.15 by
  itself, which pushed a \$10 session to \$13.88. This led to the
  per-run spend cap.
- •
  A proposer that hit the step limit had its work discarded. The kernel
  now streams results and keeps the last state.
- •
  A discovery session launched from a foreground shell lost a proposer
  run unharvested when the shell died. Sessions now run as daemon jobs.
- •
  A verification sandbox with a hard-coded 2 GB limit OOM-killed a valid
  $`n=7`$ qutrit evaluation. Verifier resources are now set per task.
- •
  Two autonomous jobs launched in the same second shared a session
  directory. Session names now carry a random suffix.
- •
  A full chip evaluation takes 10–12 minutes, and the kernel re-scores a
  parent whenever it is sampled. The verifier’s raw output is now cached
  by verifier, solution, split and image, and the score is recomputed
  from it on every read, so a corrected score range does not invalidate
  the cache.

Each of these looked minor, and each would have silently cost a result.

#### Mistakes in the chip evaluator.

The accelerator task needed four fixes from the operator before its
scores could be trusted, and two of them repeat earlier lessons.

- •
  Score range reversed. The first launch mapped the original design to a
  score of 1. We cancelled it before any proposer ran. An autonomous
  scout later made the same mistake
  (Section [3.8](#S3.SS8 "3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).
- •
  Saturation, again. In session 1 the score reached 1 at 289 fJ, half
  the baseline. Both first-round proposers beat that bound in their
  first run, so later runs had nothing to gain, and an _aggressive
  rewrite_ proposer shipped its parent unchanged. This is the AdderBoard
  saturation of
  Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
  without the gaming. We cancelled the session, set the score-1 point to
  100 fJ, and reseeded session 2 with session 1’s best design.
- •
  Silent simulation. Icarus left the internal delayed signals of the
  ASAP7 sequential cell models undriven, so the first gate-level runs
  produced no outputs at all. The evaluator now compiles functional
  versions of the cell models.
- •
  The wrong DRC count. The first parser read the DRC count from the
  first routing iteration rather than the last. It now reads the final
  count by exact key.

None of these favoured a candidate, but each would have produced wrong
numbers in the tables above if a person had not read the logs.

#### Where progress came from within a session.

Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Where progress came from within a session. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
plots every scored proposal on six problems in the order it ran, with
the best value so far. Three patterns hold across them.

- •
  Gains come early in a session. Every improvement was set in the first
  or second iteration of its session; no third-iteration run set a new
  best on any problem.
- •
  A few arms carry the gains. The runs that set new bests drew
  _aggressive rewrite_ (qutrit twice, Golay, SABRE), _new neighbourhood_
  (C11, the SABRE beam search, two LM steps), _data structure_ (SABRE),
  _structured construction_ (stabilizer rank), and _connectivity_ and
  _parameter sharing_ (the LM). _Conservative_ set a new best twice
  (SABRE, LM) and _robust/simple_ once (SABRE), only where the seed was
  far from optimal; on a record seed they never did.
- •
  Most proposals do not improve. Of 47 scored proposals on these six
  problems, 16 set a new best. The search is a sequence of rare large
  steps between plateaus, not a steady climb.

The accelerator task, which is not in the figure, fits the first two
patterns only in part. Its last and largest step came in the third
iteration of session 2, from _new neighbourhood_. A _conservative_ run
there did useful work, because the notes held a concrete untried
combination: it merged the seed’s clock gating with a parallel run’s
arithmetic (274.9 to 252.8 fJ). A second _conservative_ draw on the
188.2 fJ design shipped it unchanged.

Figure 6: Every scored proposal (dots) and the best value so far (line),
in chronological order across sessions; dashed lines mark session
boundaries, and orange dots set a new best. A session’s seed can raise
the bar between sessions when the operator combined earlier runs (the
SABRE per-circuit merge). Values are those the kernel recorded for each
run: (a) the claimed float threshold (the certified point is 0.064966);
(c) two-qubit gates $`+\,0.1\times`$ depth; (d) $`12/\text{value}`$,
i.e. the number of stabilizer states; (e) per-run mean ratio to SABRE,
before the host’s per-circuit combination (0.5073); (f) excludes four
session-2 runs stopped by the Modal spend limit. Extracted from the run
banks.

#### Cost.

The fourteen problem campaigns used about \$171 of LLM usage, and about
\$180 with the gated evolve run, plus Modal compute. The three
autonomous runs cost a further \$27.42 end to end, and the accelerator
campaign \$11.0 plus Modal CPU time. Single finding runs cost between
\$0.60 (the C11 state) and \$4.15 (the $`T^{\otimes 7}`$ decomposition).
Host-side certification was sometimes the expensive part: about 45
CPU-minutes per endpoint for the C11 certificate.

## 5 Safety

A system that edits its own harness and runs code it wrote needs
containment that does not rely on the model’s cooperation. The Infinity
Machine enforces the following structurally, in the kernel.

- •
  Sandboxing. Every proposer and every scorer runs in a fresh container
  or Modal sandbox. Network is off by default, the root file system is
  read-only, and data volumes, where needed, are mounted read-only.
  Kernel code, private splits, scorers and credentials are never
  mounted, so an agent cannot read its hidden grade or change how it is
  graded.
- •
  Immutable grading. The kernel scores solutions in a separate sandbox
  and never trusts an agent’s report of what it ran. A genome edit that
  touches kernel paths, or changes a kernel-owned file by a single byte,
  is rejected before grading.
- •
  Bounded spend. A per-run cap ends an agent at its next model call once
  its cost reaches the limit, and a session budget stops new proposers.
- •
  Human gates and their machine replacement. A self-modification whose
  gain exceeds the anomaly threshold is parked for review instead of
  activated. Every generation can be rolled back. Outside autonomous
  mode, proposed evaluators are inert until a human approves them. In
  autonomous mode that approval is automatic only after three checks:
  kernel calibration on known cases, an adversarial audit whose exploits
  are replayed, and a blind independent re-check of the final result.
  The approval and its basis are logged. A verifier written by one agent
  is therefore never trusted on that agent’s word alone. In the first of
  the three autonomous runs, this chain rejected the first task.
- •
  No outward actions. Agents cannot publish. Every external step in this
  paper was taken by the operator: the Zenodo deposits, the catalogue
  issues and pull requests, and the arena posts. Autonomous mode has
  network access only in the scout and audit phases, to read catalogues
  and the literature, and it ends with a report, not a submission.

What we observed is mostly in
Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research").
Proposers gamed lenient scorers four times, and in two cases said so
openly: once when asked for review risks (AdderBoard), and once in a
notebook (TESS). We saw no attempt to read hidden splits or to escape a
sandbox. However, unlike STOP \[[3](#bib.bib3)\], we did not audit
traces systematically for such attempts, so this is an absence of
observed incidents, not a measured rate. The main residual risk is not
the agent but the harness: our private splits were only as good as the
verifiers the operator wrote, and two of them were exploitable for a
full iteration before they were fixed.

## 6 Related work

#### LLM-guided program search.

FunSearch \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] evolved short Python functions scored by an
evaluator. AlphaEvolve \[[1](#bib.bib1)\] scaled this to whole files,
rich prompts and many problems, and Georgiev et al. \[[39](#bib.bib39)\]
applied it to 67 problems in mathematical analysis, geometry and
combinatorics. ShinkaEvolve \[[40](#bib.bib40)\] and
Hyra \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] are open, sample-efficient variants; Hyra uses
agentic proposers and lets the evaluator evolve.
AIDE \[[41](#bib.bib41)\] searches over ML code with a tree of drafts.
The Infinity Machine shares their reliance on automatic evaluation but
differs in kind: its proposals are hour-long agent runs rather than
sampled programs, it also searches open-endedly in real data, and its
own harness is subject to gated self-modification.

#### Self-improving agents.

STOP \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] improved its own scaffolding program. The Darwin
Gödel Machine \[[4](#bib.bib4)\] evolved coding agents with an archive
and documented reward hacking of its own tests.
Hyperagents \[[5](#bib.bib5)\] made the meta agent editable.
AIDE² \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] rewrote a research agent’s harness under a
private grade it never sees. Prime Agent \[[42](#bib.bib42)\] and
Continual Harness \[[43](#bib.bib43)\] keep typed supplemental state
with rollback by ID, building on recursive language
models \[[44](#bib.bib44)\]. ACE \[[11](#bib.bib11)\] curates an
itemised playbook. Weng \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] surveys harness engineering
for self-improvement. The Infinity Machine combines an editable meta
agent, an archive, a cost-aware gate and an ACE-style playbook, and adds
an honest report that, so far, its discovery results come from the
unmodified genome.

#### Agents for science.

ReAct \[[45](#bib.bib45)\] and Reflexion \[[46](#bib.bib46)\]
established tool use and verbal feedback. The AI
Scientist \[[47](#bib.bib47)\] automated the paper cycle in ML. Our
emphasis is narrower and older: a claim counts only if a program that
the agent did not write can check it.

## 7 Discussion

#### What worked.

Giving a strong model a shell, an hour and an exact verifier was enough
to move four catalogued open problems and one standard benchmark in six
days for under \$200 of model usage. The winning moves were often
changes of representation. Two were not suggested anywhere in the
operator’s notes:

- •
  counting mixed qubits instead of non-$`Z`$ qubits (Golay);
- •
  shrinking $`n`$ instead of growing it (qutrit).

Two others implemented directions the notes listed as untried: a
symmetric dictionary instead of annealing over all stabilizer states
(stabilizer rank), and a beam over SWAP sequences instead of a greedy
SWAP choice (SABRE). The public/private split and adversarially
calibrated verifiers, not instructions, kept the outputs honest. The
same idea carried over to autonomous mode. When an agent writes its own
evaluator, the evaluator is trusted only after machine checks that a
different agent and the kernel perform. In the first end-to-end run
these checks caught a stale record that would otherwise have become a
false discovery. The approach also carried over to hardware. With power
measured from gate-level switching activity on a routed design, and
correctness checked bit-exactly at both RTL and gate level, the
proposers cut energy per MAC by 77.7% through architectural changes
(dataflow, storage structure, clock gating, generated arithmetic) rather
than tuning.

#### What did not.

Self-improvement has not yet earned its name in our data. The one
self-derived generation was rejected on cost, the most consequential
harness changes were the operator’s, and cross-session memory ran
through hand-edited notes. Where a record is a robust optimum of
random-restart search (MUBs, Hadamard, the seven-qubit code), the
Infinity Machine reproduced the record and produced negative evidence,
not progress. Proposers sometimes found an object without understanding
it, as with the product structure of the qutrit state. All three fully
autonomous runs ended in ties with public records. The first scout chose
a crowded problem, and the first run’s final round was wasted on
conservative no-ops. Research arms and narrower goals in runs 2 and 3
produced real searches and near misses, but no improvement, and two
proposers still declined to search. In run 2 the machine checks that
replace human approval passed a task whose score was reversed. They test
whether a verifier accepts the right objects, but not whether the score
ranks them the right way round.

#### Limitations.

All results come from a single operator, a single proposer model and one
to three sessions per problem. There are no repeated seeds, ablations or
matched-compute comparisons. Several problems were chosen _because_ they
looked search-shaped, so the success rate is not representative. The
quantum results are lower bounds or explicit constructions with stated
claim boundaries, not optimality results. The SABRE comparison is not
compute-matched. The TESS candidate is unconfirmed. The accelerator
result rests on a predictive PDK, one flow, one clock, one synthetic
workload and zero-delay gate-level simulation, and it compares against
the original RTL rather than a hand-optimised design. End-to-end
autonomy has been demonstrated three times, all with null results, and
in runs 2 and 3 the operator named the table to search. The fifteen
operator-led campaigns that produced the results above were not run in
autonomous mode, so none of their results is an autonomous end-to-end
discovery.

#### Next steps.

Next we plan to: run autonomous mode repeatedly with open goals, with a
scout that also checks leaderboards and discussion threads before
choosing, a validation step that checks the score’s direction on
calibration cases, and a brief that forbids returning the parent without
a search; repeat the accelerator task on a second PDK, at several clocks
and workload seeds, with timing-annotated simulation; let the meta agent
propose strategy arms and brief templates through the gate; replace
operator-written “already measured” tables with consolidation output,
and measure whether the next session does better; run matched A/B
comparisons of gated generations on held-out problem families
(imp@$`k`$ \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]); and add a reviewer round to every
catalogue-mode session.

## Use of AI systems

The discoveries reported here were made by Claude Sonnet 5.5 proposer
agents inside the Infinity Machine. The harness, task verifiers, seeds,
figure scripts and this manuscript were written by the author with the
assistance of Claude (Anthropic) as a coding and writing assistant,
under the author’s direction. The author chose the problems, checked
every reported number on the host, and takes responsibility for the
content.

## Data availability

States, circuits, decompositions, routings, certificates, agent
notebooks and verification code for the published results are on
Zenodo \[[12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13), [14](#bib.bib14),
[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17),
[18](#bib.bib18)\]. The accelerator designs, evaluator and notebooks,
and the three autonomous session directories, are not yet deposited.

## Ethics statement

The problems studied are in mathematics, quantum information, compilers,
machine learning, astronomy and digital hardware design, and carry
little direct potential for harm. The broader concern with
self-improving agents is that they may optimise a proxy in unintended
ways. We observed exactly this on a small scale
(Section [4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3 "Specification gaming within one iteration. ‣ 4 What the loop learned, and what it did not ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research"))
and report every instance. All external claims went out under the
author’s name after host-side verification, with AI involvement
disclosed in each deposit, and none was posted by an agent. The TESS
candidate is reported as unconfirmed, and no follow-up request was sent
on the agent’s behalf.

## Reproducibility statement

For every published result, the Zenodo deposits contain the solution
object, the verifier, the task text given to the agents, the agents’
notebooks and search code, and SHA-256 sums. Anyone can re-check the
results without our harness.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Discovery sessions ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
lists every discovery session with its configuration and spend,
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Strategy arms ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
the strategy-arm texts, and
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Gate configuration and the self-derived playbook ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
the gate configuration and the self-derived playbook. For each
autonomous run, the session directory keeps every artefact: the goal,
each scout round’s task, the validation reports, both audits with their
exploit files and replay results, the automatic approval record, the
search bank, the independent checker’s code and verdict, and the final
report and claim.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B The autonomous runs in detail ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
summarises it. Model runs are not deterministic: rerunning a session
will produce different proposals, and we report only one session
sequence per problem. The model versions were Claude Sonnet 5.5 for
proposers and Claude Opus 5.5 for the meta agent.

## Appendix A Details of each discovery

For every result in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")
we give the definition, the known results, the result, how it was found
and how it was verified. “How it was found” identifies the run that
produced the object: session and run identifiers, start time (UTC,
October 2026), strategy arm, model, wall time, tokens and model cost,
all from the kernel’s run records. It then gives the method with its
parameters, as recorded in the proposer’s notebook, and the search
effort, including what was tried without success. “Verification” lists
each check separately: what was checked, by which program and by whom,
the acceptance criterion and the outcome, followed by a command that
reproduces it from the Zenodo deposit. All proposers are Claude
Sonnet 5.5.

### A.1 Quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel

Let $`\mathcal{D}_{p}(\rho)=(1-3p)\rho+p(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z)`$,
with $`p`$ the per-Pauli error probability. By the Lloyd–Shor–Devetak
theorem, $`Q(\mathcal{D}_{p})>0`$ whenever some input $`\rho`$ on $`n`$
channel uses has positive coherent information
$`I_{c}(\rho,\mathcal{D}_{p}^{\otimes n})=S(\mathcal{D}_{p}^{\otimes n}(\rho))-S((\mathcal{D}_{p}^{\otimes n}\otimes\mathrm{id})(\psi_{\rho}))`$,
where $`\psi_{\rho}`$ purifies $`\rho`$. The threshold
$`p^{*}=\sup\{p:Q(\mathcal{D}_{p})>0\}`$ is unknown (catalogue entry
C11 \[[48](#bib.bib48)\]). Known lower bounds include
$`0.0637675`$ \[[19](#bib.bib19)\] and
$`0.064912`$ \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]. The best certified point was
$`p=16239/250000=0.064956`$, for a 45-copy rank-two input supported on
the symmetric subspace, certified in exact rational
arithmetic \[[21](#bib.bib21)\].

#### Result.

A 45-qubit rank-two input on the symmetric subspace whose coherent
information is certified positive at $`p=32483/500000=0.064966`$, which
raises the certified point by $`1.0\times 10^{-5}`$. Its fidelity with
the previous record state is $`0.99927`$.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. Session 20261019-181124, iteration 0, proposer 0. Started 18:11;
  _new neighbourhood_ arm; 2,522 s; 181,073 input and 3,457 output
  tokens; \$0.60.
- •
  Start. The record state A, given as the seed (kernel score 0.478). The
  tools were the operator’s float evaluator, which reduces $`I_{c}`$ for
  symmetric-subspace inputs to Schur–Weyl blocks via a coherent-state
  generating function and never forms a $`2^{n}`$-dimensional matrix,
  and its autograd twin.
- •
  Method. The proposer wrote its own checkpointing Adam polish on the
  real and imaginary parts of the two unnormalised Dicke-basis rows
  (learning rate $`5\times 10^{-5}`$). It worked at a fixed $`p`$ and
  raised $`p`$ by $`10^{-6}`$ whenever $`I_{c}>2\times 10^{-9}`$, for
  about 5,600 steps, writing the current state to /work/solution
  throughout.
- •
  Delivered. A claimed $`p=0.064967`$ and kernel score 0.4835.
- •
  Also tried. A second iteration (\$0.72) tried a third row of norm 0.03
  (rank three) and a Dicke lift to $`n=46`$. Neither beat the delivered
  state.

#### Verification.

1.  1.  Kernel. The task verifier ran in a fresh sandbox. It accepts a
        claimed $`p`$ only if $`I_{c}>10^{-11}`$ in two independent
        quadrature bases (Fibonacci-sphere points). Outcome: accepted at
        $`p=0.064967`$.
2.  2.  Float scan (operator). $`I_{c}=+2.63\times 10^{-7}`$,
        $`+1.21\times 10^{-7}`$, $`+2.58\times 10^{-8}`$,
        $`+2.05\times 10^{-9}`$ and $`-2.17\times 10^{-8}`$ bits at
        $`p=0.064956`$, $`0.064962`$, $`0.064966`$, $`0.064967`$ and
        $`0.064968`$. The float threshold is therefore
        $`\approx 0.0649671`$.
3.  3.  Exact certificate. The record authors’ certifier
        (certified_coherent_information; rational arithmetic, 224-bit
        square-root enclosures, 50-digit directed accumulation) was run
        unchanged on the host, taking 8,407 s and 8,361 s:

    | $`p`$ (exact)             | certified enclosure of $`I_{c}`$ (bits) | float evaluator          |
    | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
    | $`32481/500000=0.064962`$ | $`[1.1807,\,1.2256]\times 10^{-7}`$     | $`1.2062\times 10^{-7}`$ |
    | $`32483/500000=0.064966`$ | $`[2.3084,\,2.7775]\times 10^{-8}`$     | $`2.5763\times 10^{-8}`$ |

    Both endpoints are classified certified-positive, and each float
    value lies inside its enclosure. Since $`I_{c}`$ is nonincreasing in
    $`p`$ for a fixed input, $`Q(\mathcal{D}_{p})>0`$ for all
    $`p\leq 0.064966`$.

4.  4.  Reproduce. The state is payloads/EVO1.c128 (complex128, shape
        $`2\times 46`$, 1,472 bytes, SHA-256 7f11f2f1…67c5ae). Run python
        certify.py ../payloads/EVO1.c128 0.064966 out.json (about 45
        CPU-minutes) \[[12](#bib.bib12)\].

### A.2 Positivity frontier of the qutrit depolarizing channel

Let $`\mathcal{N}_{d,p}(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+p\,I/d`$. For $`d\geq 3`$ the
catalogue (QIQC zoo \[[49](#bib.bib49)\]) listed only the hashing point,
i.e. the zero of $`I_{c}`$ for the maximally mixed input, which for
$`d=3`$ is $`p_{h}=0.287087`$.

#### Result.

With $`\eta(x)=-x\log_{2}x`$ and $`\sigma_{2}`$ the maximally mixed
state on a two-dimensional subspace of $`\mathbb{C}^{d}`$,

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
I_{c}(\sigma_{2},\mathcal{N}_{d,p})=2\,\eta\!\Big(\tfrac{1-p}{2}+\tfrac{p}{d}\Big)+(d-2)\,\eta\!\Big(\tfrac{p}{d}\Big)-\eta\!\Big(1-p+\tfrac{p}{2d}\Big)-(2d-1)\,\eta\!\Big(\tfrac{p}{2d}\Big),
``` |  |

whose zero for $`d=3`$ lies in
$`[0.29106723603359969,\ 0.29106723603359988]`$. This is above the
hashing point by $`3.98\times 10^{-3}`$. The same single-letter gain
holds for every $`3\leq d\leq 64`$ that we checked, for example $`d=4`$:
$`0.3170689`$ against $`0.3089806`$.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Session 1 run. Session 20261020-025047, iteration 0, proposer 0.
  Started 03:01; *aggressive rewrite*; 1,934 s; 993,698 input and 19,509
  output tokens; \$3.27.

  - –
    *Start:* the seed, a rank-3 repetition input on $`n=7`$ (threshold
    $`0.287731`$), with the operator’s exact brute-force evaluator
    ($`n\leq 7`$, rank $`\leq 4`$) and its autograd twin.
  - –
    *Method:* a rank-4 input on $`n=4`$ built from the repetition rows
    plus a small noisy fourth row. It ran Adam at fixed $`p=0.2874`$,
    taking $`I_{c}`$ from $`-5\times 10^{-4}`$ to
    $`+9.9\times 10^{-3}`$, then a warm-started $`p`$-ladder.
  - –
    *Outcome:* threshold $`0.289205`$, with two seeds agreeing to
    $`0.2892`$–$`0.2893`$.
- •
  Session 2 run (finding run). Session 20261020-040144, iteration 0,
  proposer 0. Started 04:01; *aggressive rewrite*; 1,726 s; 715,424
  input and 14,517 output tokens; \$2.36.

  - –
    *Start:* the session-1 state.
  - –
    *Observation recorded in the notebook:* with rank 4 allowed, a
    smaller $`n`$ is better.
  - –
    *Method:* Adam $`p`$-ladders from random starts gave $`n=3`$:
    $`0.28995`$ and $`n=2`$: $`0.29106`$. L-BFGS with a strong-Wolfe
    line search and a bisection ladder on $`p`$ then reached
    $`0.2910672`$, with bisection to $`\approx 4\times 10^{-8}`$.
  - –
    *Global check:* 25 random L-BFGS starts at $`n=2`$ all converge to
    the same optimum, with $`I_{c}(0.29108)=-6.5466\times 10^{-5}`$.
  - –
    *Also tried:* lifts to $`n=3,4`$ return to the $`n=2`$ value.
- •
  Operator. Computed the reduced states, found the product structure
  $`\sigma_{2}\otimes\sigma_{2}`$ and derived the closed form above. Two
  later proposer runs had observed that the state is $`P/4`$ on a
  subspace, but neither computed the reduced states.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Kernel. The exact brute-force verifier, run in a fresh sandbox,
    accepts if $`I_{c}>10^{-10}`$ at the claimed $`p`$. Outcome: value
    $`0.2910672`$, score 0.81344.
2.  2.
    Host bisection. Bisection to $`10^{-8}`$ gives $`0.29106723`$, with
    $`I_{c}(0.2910672)=+1.848181\times 10^{-7}`$ and
    $`I_{c}(0.291068)=-3.92\times 10^{-6}`$ bits.
3.  3.
    High precision. A 30-digit mpmath recomputation at the stored
    amplitudes gives $`1.84818087\times 10^{-7}`$ bits. The smallest
    joint eigenvalue is $`2.4\times 10^{-3}`$, so the entropies are
    smooth there.
4.  4.
    Structure.
    $`\lVert\rho-\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B}\rVert=3\times 10^{-9}`$, and
    both reduced spectra are $`(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2},0)`$. The
    closed form agrees with the evaluator.
5.  5.
    Interval certificate. mpmath.iv at 50 digits gives the enclosure
    stated above.
6.  6.
    Reproduce. python rank2_certificate.py, and python
    verification/highprec_check.py
    states/s2-it00-p0_n2r4_p0.2910672.json 0.2910672 30 (state SHA-256
    4c3802af…) \[[13](#bib.bib13)\].

The result is elementary enough that it may be known, and no priority is
claimed.

### A.3 Private information of the qubit depolarizing channel

For $`\Lambda_{p}(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+p\,I/2`$, the zoo record certified
$`P(\Lambda_{p})>0`$ only for $`p\leq 0.259824`$. The single-use
six-state ensemble with noisy preprocessing \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] has
positive private information below $`p=0.28223`$.

#### Result.

Explicit two-member classical ensembles on $`n`$ qubits with positive
private information $`I(X;B)-I(X;E)`$ at
$`p=0.28336,0.28372,0.28405,0.28437,0.28466`$ for $`n=4,\dots,8`$. At
$`n=8`$, member 0 is $`\rho_{0}=\sum_{s}w_{s}|s\rangle\langle s|`$ with
$`w_{s}\propto e^{f_{|s|}}`$, where the logits over Hamming weight
$`0,\dots,8`$ are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
f=(0.9295,\,-0.8515,\,-1.8970,\,-2.2646,\,-2.4467,\,-2.4550,\,-2.1969,\,-1.1514,\,0.6337).
``` |  |

Member 1 is its bit complement, and the two members have equal priors.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. Session 20261020-201046, iteration 0, proposer 1. Started 20:11;
  *new neighbourhood*; 2,635 s; 630,192 input and 14,966 output tokens;
  \$2.12.
- •
  Start. The session-1 $`n=5`$ ensemble (threshold $`0.283722`$), found
  by Adam on all $`2^{n}`$ logits.
- •
  Method. The proposer restricted the ensemble to a classical complement
  pair whose weights are a softmax over $`n+1`$ Hamming-weight logits.
  This reduces the environment entropy to $`n+1`$ eigenproblems. It then
  ran Adam in torch on the exact classical private information,
  cross-checked against the verifier, with continuation in $`p`$ and a
  final bisection.
- •
  Outcome. Thresholds $`0.28336`$, $`0.28372`$, $`0.28406`$, $`0.28437`$
  and $`0.28467`$ for $`n=4,\dots,8`$.
- •
  Also tried. Three, four, six and eight classical members at $`n=3,4`$
  (no gain). General complex members at $`n=2,3`$, started at the
  classical optimum, do not exceed it, and random starts collapse to
  zero private information.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Kernel. The verifier accepts if the private information is at least
    $`10^{-9}`$ bits at the claimed $`p`$. The evaluator self-tests
    reproduce the hashing rate, brute-force Stinespring results for
    $`n\leq 3`$, and the 14.11% Renes–Smith rate.
2.  2.
    Host. Thresholds by bisection in double precision; at $`n=8`$ the
    threshold is $`0.2846707`$, and the private information at
    $`p=0.28466`$ is $`2.5\times 10^{-7}`$ bits.
3.  3.
    High precision. A 30-digit mpmath recomputation was made for every
    deposited ensemble ($`n=8`$ takes about 10 minutes).
4.  4.
    Reproduce. python verify/private_info.py
    ensembles/n8_shell_symmetric.json and python verify/certify_mp.py
    ensembles/n5_shell_symmetric.json 30 \[[15](#bib.bib15)\].

The literature already implies $`P>0`$ up to $`p\approx 0.2915`$; that
is the operator’s argument, given in the deposit. These ensembles are
new only as explicit finite-$`n`$ witnesses.

### A.4 Preparing the Golay logical zero

The task is to prepare
$`|0_{G}\rangle=2^{-11/2}\sum_{c\in C^{\perp}}|c\rangle`$ of the
$`[[23,1,7]]`$ Golay code from $`|0\rangle^{\otimes 23}`$ with Clifford
gates, no ancillas and free single-qubit gates, minimising the two-qubit
gate count $`N`$ and the two-qubit depth $`D`$. The published Pareto
points were $`(N,D)=(45,7)`$ and $`(44,8)`$ from RL plus MCTS graph
decimation \[[24](#bib.bib24)\], and earlier $`(57,7)`$, $`(56,17)`$ and
$`(45,10)`$.

#### Result.

A circuit with $`N=44`$ controlled-$`Z`$ gates in $`D=6`$ layers, which
dominates both published points. In the cyclic coordinates of the Golay
code, its two-qubit layers are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{1}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ (4,10),(17,15),(20,16),(1,8),(13,21),(18,6),(12,11),(5,3),(0,14)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{2}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ (2,16),(8,10),(17,6),(1,12),(11,21),(15,0),(18,13),(5,22),(9,3),(7,20)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{3}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ (8,19),(12,17),(11,0),(14,22),(6,4),(3,13),(7,21)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{4}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ (12,5),(19,16),(0,2),(22,8),(4,21),(3,20)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{5}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ (16,12),(10,0),(18,19),(6,2),(20,11),(4,9),(21,22)`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{6}`$ | $`\displaystyle:\ (5,10),(4,11),(9,16),(2,21),(3,6).`$ |  |

The interleaved single-qubit Cliffords are in the
deposit \[[14](#bib.bib14)\].

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. Session 20261020-163836, iteration 1, proposer 1. Started 17:03;
  *aggressive rewrite*; 1,491 s; 815,918 input and 27,297 output tokens;
  \$2.86.
- •
  Start. The operator’s transcription of the published $`(44,8)`$
  circuit.
- •
  Representation. The circuit is written as 44 controlled-Pauli gates
  $`\mathrm{CP}(a,b,P,Q)`$ in a global Pauli frame, so all single-qubit
  Cliffords are absorbed. A stabilizer tableau stored as 46 32-bit
  columns, written in C, evaluates about $`5\times 10^{6}`$ full
  circuits per second per core (the previous Python version ran at
  49,000).
- •
  Cost. The number of qubits left mixed when the circuit is applied in
  reverse to the target. A qubit is pure if and only if its $`X`$- and
  $`Z`$-columns are linearly dependent, so cost 0 means a product state
  in any local basis. The previous session’s cost accepted only
  $`Z`$-basis product states.
- •
  Search. A Metropolis walk at a fixed 44 gates ($`T=0.3`$) with energy
  $`2\cdot\text{cost}+\#\{\text{gates in layers beyond the target depth}\}`$.
  Its moves change a gate’s Pauli axes or endpoints, shift it in the
  order, replace it, or delete one gate and insert another. From the
  start circuit it reaches depth $`\leq 7`$ in about 1 s and depth
  $`\leq 6`$ in 10–60 s. A converter turns the result back into H, S and
  CZ gates with Pauli sign fixes.
- •
  Not found. Depth 5: in four runs of 300 s, the best is one gate over
  the layer limit. 43 gates:

  - –
    an exhaustive delete-two/insert-one scan of 92 million neighbours of
    the start circuit has minimum cost 2;
  - –
    four fixed-length-43 annealing runs of 540 s each, about $`10^{10}`$
    evaluations in total, end at cost 2, i.e. one Bell pair left.

  Total compute was about 25 CPU-minutes.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Kernel. The verifier (golay_core.check_circuit) ran in a fresh
    sandbox and simulates the circuit as a stabilizer tableau. The
    output group is CSS, with pure-$`X`$ rank 11 and pure-$`Z`$ rank 12;
    all signs are $`+`$; and the $`Z`$-code has minimum distance 7,
    which makes it the Golay code by uniqueness. It reported $`N=44`$
    and earliest-possible (ASAP) depth 6; value $`44.6`$.
2.  2.
    Relabelling (operator). find_relabeling.py finds the wire
    permutation $`\pi`$ to the cyclic coordinates. It is the same
    permutation as for the published start circuit, and the relabelled
    circuit prepares the cyclic-code state exactly.
3.  3.
    Statevector. A full $`2^{23}`$-amplitude simulation gives overlap
    $`1.0`$ with $`|0_{G}\rangle`$ in cyclic coordinates.
4.  4.
    Reproduce. python verify/golay_core.py
    circuits/evo_44_depth6_cyclic.json --sv (a few seconds; about 130 MB
    of memory).

### A.5 Stabilizer rank of $`|T\rangle^{\otimes 7}`$

For $`|T\rangle=(|0\rangle+e^{i\pi/4}|1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}`$, the
stabilizer rank $`\chi(\psi)`$ is the least number of stabilizer states
whose span contains $`\psi`$. The exact values
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes m})`$ are known for $`m\leq 4`$
($`2,2,3,4`$) \[[25](#bib.bib25)\]. For $`m=5,6`$ the bounds were
$`6`$ \[[26](#bib.bib26)\], and for $`m=7`$ only the product bound
$`12`$.

#### Result.

With $`\zeta=e^{i\pi/4}`$,
$`|T\rangle^{\otimes 7}=2^{-7/2}\sum_{j=1}^{10}c_{j}|\varphi_{j}\rangle`$
for the ten stabilizer states below. They are written in Dehaene–De Moor
form
$`|\varphi\rangle=\sum_{y\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{k}}i^{e(y)}|x_{0}+Gy\rangle`$,
with $`e(y)=\sum_{i}a_{i}y_{i}+2\sum_{(i,l)\in B}y_{i}y_{l}`$, where the
columns of $`G`$ are the vectors $`g_{1},\dots,g_{k}`$. Hence
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 7})\leq 10`$, and by sub-multiplicativity
$`\chi(|T\rangle^{\otimes 13})\leq 60`$ (previously 72).

| $`j`$ | $`k`$ | $`x_{0}`$ |  $`g_{1},\dots,g_{k}`$ | $`a`$ |  $`B`$ | $`c_{j}`$ |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| 1 | 1 | 0011111 |  1111111 | (2) |  – | $`-2\zeta-2\zeta^{2}`$ |
| 2 | 4 | 0000001 |  0010001, 0001001, 0000101, 0000011 | (0,0,0,0) |  – | $`\zeta`$ |
| 3 | 4 | 1100000 |  0010001, 0001001, 0000101, 0000011 | (0,0,0,0) |  – | $`-1+\zeta-\zeta^{3}`$ |
| 4 | 3 | 0000000 |  1000000, 0100000, 0011111 | (2,2,1) |  – | $`1-\zeta`$ |
| 5 | 3 | 0000000 |  1000000, 0100000, 0011111 | (0,0,1) |  all pairs | $`1+\zeta`$ |
| 6 | 7 | 0000000 |  $`I_{7}`$ | (0,0,1,1,1,1,1) |  – | $`\tfrac{1}{4}(1-\zeta-\zeta^{2}-\zeta^{3})`$ |
| 7 | 7 | 0000000 |  $`I_{7}`$ | (0,0,0,0,0,0,0) |  – | $`\tfrac{1}{2}(-\zeta+\zeta^{3})`$ |
| 8 | 7 | 0000000 |  $`I_{7}`$ | (0,0,1,1,1,1,1) |  $`(1,l),l>1`$; $`(2,l),l>2`$ | $`\tfrac{1}{4}(-1-\zeta+\zeta^{2}-\zeta^{3})`$ |
| 9 | 6 | 0000000 |  1000001, 0100001, 0010001, 0001001, 0000101, 0000011 | (0,0,0,0,0,0) |  (1,2) | $`\tfrac{1}{2}(-1+\zeta+\zeta^{2}-\zeta^{3})`$ |
| 10 | 5 | 0000000 |  1100001, 0010001, 0001001, 0000101, 0000011 | (0,2,2,2,2) |  all pairs | $`\tfrac{1}{2}(-1+\zeta-\zeta^{2}+\zeta^{3})`$ |

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. Session 20261021-033358, iteration 0, proposer 0. Started 03:34;
  *structured construction*; 1,603 s; 1,216,380 input and 33,582 output
  tokens; \$4.15. The run stopped at the \$4 per-run cap.
- •
  Dictionary. The qubits are split into blocks $`[a,b]`$ with $`a+b=7`$.
  Three states (the all-zero state, a block GHZ state and the global GHZ
  state) are closed under all $`S_{a}\times S_{b}`$-symmetric Cliffords:
  block-wise H, S and X, CZ within and between blocks, and block-parity
  CNOT fans. This gives 396–540 vectors, which span the
  $`(a+1)(b+1)`$-dimensional symmetric space for $`[2,5]`$, $`[3,4]`$
  and other partitions, but not for $`[1,6]`$ or the fully symmetric
  case.
- •
  Subset search. Batched simulated annealing over $`r`$-subsets of the
  dictionary, minimising the squared least-squares residual of
  $`|T\rangle^{\otimes 7}`$, with 1,024 chains at about $`10^{6}`$
  evaluations per minute per CPU. It reached $`r=12`$ on $`[3,4]`$ in
  40 s, $`r=11`$ on $`[3,4]`$ in 220 s and on $`[2,5]`$ in 130 s, and
  then $`r=10`$ on $`[2,5]`$. Solutions were converted to exact normal
  form and checked with the exact verifier.
- •
  Record note. The header of the run’s notebook still reports $`r=11`$;
  it was written before $`r=10`$ was found. The delivered solution.json
  contains 10 states.
- •
  Also tried. An exhaustive $`\mathbb{Z}_{5}`$-orbit test over all 2.4
  million five-qubit stabilizer states found no single cyclic orbit of
  five states containing $`|T\rangle^{\otimes 5}`$. Separately, a
  companion *exhaustive small case* run stalled at residual 0.0647 for
  five terms at $`m=5`$.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Kernel. Exact Gaussian elimination over
    $`\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)=\mathbb{Q}[\zeta]/(\zeta^{4}+1)`$ confirms that
    $`|T\rangle^{\otimes 7}`$ lies in the span of the ten states. Value
    $`12/10=1.2`$.
2.  2.
    Independent check (operator, separate code). The stabilizer group of
    each state, found by brute force over all 16,384 Pauli operators,
    has order $`2^{7}`$. A 40-digit least-squares residual is
    $`1.6\times 10^{-41}`$. The exact coefficients lie in
    $`\tfrac{1}{4}\mathbb{Z}[\zeta]`$ and agree with least squares to
    $`10^{-9}`$.
3.  3.
    Reproduce. python verify/stabrank.py decomposition/T7_rank10.json
    and python verify/independent_check.py decomposition/T7_rank10.json
    (seconds) \[[16](#bib.bib16)\].
````
