#### How it was found.

Six runs, all started from the previous best:

- •
  Session 1 (20261021-041641).

  - –
    *it00-p0* (*data structure*, \$3.74): SABRE rewritten in C++ over
    the two-qubit dependency graph, with early abort once a trial
    exceeds the best count (about 3,400 trials/s on adr4_197). Heuristic
    parameters ($`W`$, $`|E|`$, decay) are randomised per restart,
    followed by a hill-climb over initial mappings that swaps two
    physical qubits and accepts if not worse. Total 36,435.
  - –
    *it01-p0* (*aggressive rewrite*, 1,335 s, \$2.43): a
    receding-horizon router. At every 100-gate boundary it rolls out
    $`K`$ randomised 300-gate SABRE continuations and commits the first
    100 gates of the best; $`K`$ adapts to the remaining time. Total
    24,228.
- •
  Session 2 (20261021-053321).

  - –
    *it00-p1* (*new neighbourhood*, 2,302 s, 965,052 input and 22,692
    output tokens, \$3.24): beam.cpp, a level-synchronous beam search
    over SWAP sequences.

    - \*
      Each state is the logical-to-physical mapping plus a per-qubit
      count of executed two-qubit gates (40 bytes, hash-de-duplicated).
    - \*
      After every SWAP, all executable gates are executed greedily.
    - \*
      States are scored by
      $`\sum_{q}\sum_{j<K}\delta^{j}(\mathrm{dist}_{j}-1)-C\cdot\#\text{executed}`$,
      where $`\mathrm{dist}_{j}`$ is the distance between the qubits of
      $`q`$’s $`j`$-th upcoming gate, with $`K=6`$–$`12`$,
      $`\delta=0.7`$ and $`C\approx 1`$.
    - \*
      Beams hold up to 30,000 states, and forward–reverse passes refine
      the initial mapping.

    Total 13,050.
  - –
    *it01-p0* (*aggressive rewrite*, \$3.99): an independent beam
    variant B. The per-circuit combination of both is 12,261.
- •
  Session 3 (20261021-180153).

  - –
    *it00-p1* (*data structure*, 1,669 s, \$1.56): forward–reverse
    iteration of variant B (for example co14_215 1,926 to 1,785).
  - –
    *it02-p0* (*aggressive rewrite*): restarts of the first beam from
    perturbed initial mappings (qft_16 99, qft_20 180, misex1_241 228).

The final routing takes, per circuit, the best verified run (column
“source” in the deposit).

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Kernel. An exact replay (qmap.verify_routed) ran in a fresh sandbox
    for every run. It checks that every original gate is executed
    exactly once, after its predecessors on both qubits, on a
    coupling-graph edge under the current mapping, and that every SWAP
    acts on an edge. It then counts SWAPs.
2.  2.
    Host. The same replay on the combined routing gives a total of
    12,087.
3.  3.
    Baselines. Qiskit 2.4.1 and pytket 2.18.5 (versions pinned) ran on
    identical inputs with SWAPs counted the same way, BRIDGE counted as
    $`+3`$.
4.  4.
    Reproduce. python qmap.py verify routings/best_combined.json, which
    prints total_g_add 12087 in about a minute using only the standard
    library \[[17](#bib.bib17)\].

### A.7 The smallest adder transformer

AdderBoard \[[29](#bib.bib29)\] asks for the smallest transformer, by
parameter count, that adds two 10-digit numbers with at least 99%
accuracy. Self-attention is required, and parameters are counted by the
board’s rules (our kernel counter is stricter: constants that act as
weights count).

#### Result.

A 5-parameter, one-layer, two-head model that is correct on 10,010 of
10,010 additions on each of three seeds. Its parameters are
$`\omega=2\pi/10`$ (scalar embedding $`\omega\cdot\text{token}`$, tied
to the cosine read-out), $`\lambda=60`$ (attention sharpness),
$`\kappa=30`$ (carry-gate sharpness), $`\beta=1.5\,\omega`$ (carry
threshold) and $`g=2`$ (head-A gain). The positional encoding is a fixed
sinusoid of period 11 (no parameters).

- •
  The input is laid out as $`a_{0}..a_{9},0,b_{0}..b_{9},0`$, followed
  by the generated digits fed back as tokens.
- •
  Head A, at phase $`+1`$, averages the current digit pair.
- •
  Head B, at phase $`0`$, averages the previous digit pair and the
  previous output digit, which yields $`(s-o)/3`$, where $`s`$ is that
  pair’s digit sum and $`o`$ the previous output digit. This is $`9/3`$
  or $`10/3`$ exactly when a carry is due.
- •
  The sigmoid gate turns this into the carry, and the logits are
  $`\cos(g\,A+\omega\cdot\text{carry}-\omega k)`$ for digit $`k`$.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. AdderBoard session 1, 19 October, in an earlier scratch project;
  one proposer; 8 minutes; \$1.05. It had no parent: the proposer built
  the model from the task rules alone.
- •
  Method (from its final message). It chose the period-11 phase layout
  so that one head reads the current digit pair and the other the
  previous pair plus the generated digit. It set the five weights by
  hand. Its first local run timed out at 120 s because torch used 12
  threads per call; it set one thread, after which 10,000 additions take
  about 30 s.
- •
  Parallel run. A second proposer in the same session found an
  independent 6-parameter design (ReLU wrap).

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Local verifier (run by the proposer). 10,000 pairs on each of seeds
    2025 and 7: accuracy 1.0000, 5 counted parameters. With randomised
    weights, accuracy is 0.0.
2.  2.
    Kernel scorer (stricter counter, hidden seed). 10,000 pairs on
    hidden seed 7331, with self-attention required and the perturbation
    check repeated: passed with 5 parameters.
3.  3.
    Upstream verifier. The board’s verify.py reports QUALIFIED, 10,010
    of 10,010, on seeds 2025, 4242 and 7. Submitted as AdderBoard pull
    request \#101.

### A.8 A 20M-parameter language model

The task: an architecture of at most 20,000,000 parameters (embeddings
included), retrained by the kernel from code on 1B FineWeb-10B tokens
within 1,800 s on one H100, scored by bits per byte on the FineWeb
validation shard. The GPT-2 124M checkpoint scores 1.0658, and the seed
(a scaled-down modded-nanogpt \[[30](#bib.bib30)\], 19.36M parameters)
scores 1.3376.

#### Result.

1.2716 bits per byte with 19,146,900 parameters, which closes 24% of the
gap.

- •
  Architecture: four unique transformer blocks cycled over eight
  effective layers (two loops) at width 512 with 8 heads, and a
  factorised tied embedding of rank 128. Per-effective-layer scalars
  (residual and skip weights) are not shared, so each loop can behave
  differently.
- •
  Inherited from the session-1 parent: learnable residual/$`x_{0}`$
  mixing, U-net skips, Muon plus Adam, batch 131k tokens.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. Session 20261022-014034, iteration 0, proposer 1. Started 02:08;
  *parameter sharing*; 6,270 s including its own H100 training runs;
  360,077 input and 7,728 output tokens; \$1.20 of model usage plus GPU
  time.
- •
  Start. The session-1 best: 6 unique layers at width 448, 19.36M
  parameters, 1.2873 bits per byte when re-scored.
- •
  Experiments (one run each at the official budget).

  - –
    *A:* 12 effective layers over 4 unique blocks, width 512, embedding
    rank 96, 17.5M parameters. Time-bound: it reached only
    $`0.856\times 10^{9}`$ tokens, with validation loss 3.9586 nats.
  - –
    *B:* 8 effective layers over 4 unique blocks, width 512, rank 128,
    19.15M parameters. It reached $`0.995\times 10^{9}`$ tokens with
    loss 3.9030, against 3.9537 for the parent.

  The proposer shipped B and raised its training-time safety margin from
  45 to 80 s, because B finished at 1,770 of 1,800 s.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Kernel scorer. The scorer uploads only the code (checkpoints are
    stripped), retrains from scratch in a fresh H100 sandbox under the
    token and time limits, counts all parameters, and evaluates bits per
    byte on the FineWeb validation shard. Outcome: 1.2716, with
    19,146,900 parameters (at most 20M).
2.  2.
    Limits. One training seed; the run was not repeated.

### A.9 Low-energy 8$`\times`$8 INT8 systolic tile

The design is the LogikBench 8$`\times`$8 weight-stationary INT8
systolic array (signed 8-bit activations and weights, 32-bit outputs)
shipped as asap7/tpu with OpenROAD-flow-scripts \[[31](#bib.bib31)\]. A
tile loads eight weight rows (one per w_valid cycle), streams activation
rows, and returns each output row 15 cycles after its activation row.
The host idles $`2N-1=15`$ cycles between tiles. A candidate must keep
the ports and this cycle-level protocol, so it computes 64 MACs per
cycle at the fixed clock. There is no published record for this tile;
the reference is the original RTL.

#### Result.

An RTL rewrite (tpu.sv plus a generated mac.sv) with 128.81 fJ/MAC on
the public workload and 130.1 fJ/MAC on the private one, against
578.85 fJ/MAC for the original. At 600 ps the power is 4.34 mW internal,
3.33 mW switching and 0.04 mW leakage (7.71 mW in total, against
34.66 mW). The standard-cell area is 2,507 $`\mu`$m² (original 5,559),
setup worst slack $`+5.2`$ ps, hold worst slack $`+6.3`$ ps, and there
are 0 DRC violations.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Runs. Three runs in sequence, each building on the last:

  - –
    session 20261026-042359-discover-tpu-energy, it00-p0, *data
    structure*, started 04:40; 2,477 s, 387,077 input and 15,459 output
    tokens, \$1.39;
  - –
    session 20261026-052723-discover-tpu-energy, it00-p1, *new
    neighbourhood*, started 05:27; 3,367 s, 1,105,333 input and 24,581
    output tokens, \$3.68;
  - –
    the same session, it02-p0, *new neighbourhood*, parent it00-p1,
    started 07:02; 2,181 s, 281,823 input and 12,234 output tokens,
    \$1.03.
- •
  Tools. The operator’s evaluator (full flow, both simulations, power)
  and a quick mode of it that runs RTL simulation and synthesis only.
  Proposers ran it inside their own sandbox, so every number in their
  notebooks is a full-flow measurement.
- •
  Session 1, it00-p0. It removed the per-PE activation registers and
  broadcast each activation along its row, delaying row $`i`$ by $`7+i`$
  cycles at the input so no output de-skew is needed. It narrowed the
  partial sums to 16–19 bits per row (sign-extended at the output) and
  dropped datapath resets (346.9 fJ). It then added latch+AND clock
  gates per pipeline depth, enabled from the valid pipe derived from
  a_valid, and a w_valid gate for the weights (274.9 fJ). Flops fell
  from about 4,200 to about 2,300. A parallel run (*robust/simple*,
  \$1.81) instead wrote an explicit Baugh–Wooley multiplier with a 3:2
  carry-save tree and a Brent–Kung adder, because Yosys maps + and \* to
  Kogge–Stone structures (285.2 fJ, area 2,935).
- •
  Session 2, it00-p1. It combined the two (253.9 fJ) and tried radix-4
  Booth with activations encoded once per row (300.8 fJ, rejected). It
  then wrote a generator, gen_mac.py R, that emits one bit-level Dadda
  tree per group of $`R`$ PE rows, with Baugh–Wooley sign constants
  folded in, the incoming partial sum as an operand, and one Brent–Kung
  adder per stage. $`R=2`$ gave 210.4 fJ; $`R=4`$ (33 operands, two
  partial-sum stages, activation delay $`13+\lfloor i/4\rfloor`$) gave
  188.2 fJ, with setup slack only $`+3.6`$ ps. The proposer noted that
  $`R=8`$ would not close 600 ps.
- •
  Session 2, it02-p0. It replaced the activation shift chains (13 or 14
  stages of 64 bits, every flop toggling every cycle) by a 13-entry ring
  buffer. Each entry is written once through its own latch+AND clock
  gate under a shared one-hot pointer, and read through an AND-OR mux
  into the valid-gated input register; rows 0–3 read with the pointer
  rotated by one (delay 13), rows 4–7 without (delay 14). It also
  replaced the shifting weight register by direct per-row writes, with
  one clock gate per row and a one-hot pointer that advances on w_valid.
  Result: 128.8 fJ. An ablation in the same run (ring buffer only) gave
  144.6 fJ.
- •
  Also tried. A parallel line of runs (*conservative*, *robust/simple*,
  *data structure*) reached 252.8 fJ by the same combination, 250.2 fJ
  with a hybrid final adder (ripple-carry for the low 6 bits, Brent–Kung
  above), and 207.0 fJ with two PE rows fused per stage. Its
  *robust/simple* proposer declined to ship a 10-bit-ripple variant at
  246.2 fJ because its hold slack was $`+0.197`$ ps. Untried, per the
  final notebook: a 12-entry ring for rows 0–3, gating the pointer clock
  when idle, latch storage entries, and a ring for the partial-sum
  stages.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    RTL equivalence (kernel). Icarus Verilog simulation of the candidate
    RTL against the Python golden model on a correctness set (10 uniform
    random tiles of 16 rows, plus corner tiles: all $`-128`$, all 127,
    alternating extremes, zeros) and on the scoring workload (8 tiles of
    32 rows). Criterion: every output row bit-exact. Outcome: pass, on
    both seeds.
2.  2.
    Gate-level equivalence (kernel). The scoring workload on the routed
    netlist, with functional (zero-delay) ASAP7 cell models. Criterion:
    bit-exact. Outcome: pass, on both seeds.
3.  3.
    Physical gates (kernel). Setup and hold worst slack at the finish
    stage $`\geq 0`$, final detailed-route DRC count 0, area
    $`\leq 6{,}115.1~\mu`$m². Outcome: $`+5.2`$, $`+6.3`$ ps, 0 and
    2,507 $`\mu`$m².
4.  4.
    Power (kernel). OpenSTA read_vcd on the gate-level VCD of the
    456-cycle window and report_power with the routed SPEF; energy per
    MAC $`=P_{\text{total}}\times 456\times 600~\text{ps}/16{,}384`$.
    Public seed 2026: 128.81 fJ. Private seed 7331, run by the kernel in
    its own sandbox: 130.1 fJ.
5.  5.
    Scope. The design relies on weight loads of exactly eight w_valid
    cycles per tile, as its notebook states. The testbench always loads
    that way, so both equivalence checks hold only under this protocol.
    There was no separate host re-run beyond the kernel’s two splits.

### A.10 TESS planet candidate

#### Result.

G 249-11 (TIC 417732194; Gaia DR3 484671464331349632), an M4.5 dwarf at
29.1 pc. The candidate has $`P=5.307425\pm 0.000008`$ d,
$`T_{0}=2459912.3151\pm 0.0008`$ BJD_(TDB), depth $`3.0\pm 0.4`$ ppt,
$`T_{14}=0.88`$ h, $`b=0.83`$ and $`R_{p}=1.61\pm 0.09\,R_{\oplus}`$.

#### How it was found.

- •
  Run. Session 20261022-221142, iteration 0, proposer 0. Started 22:11
  on 22 October; *new population* arm; 6,294 s; \$7.06 (task-level
  per-run cap \$8).
- •
  Method. A box least-squares (BLS) search of TESS-SPOC full-frame-image
  light curves of the 3,100 brightest of 7,474 M dwarfs within 40 pc. It
  re-found the known planets TOI-1266, TOI-1640 and TOI-1685 at SNR
  22–23, and set aside about 1,300 referee-accepted peaks as stellar
  rotation.
- •
  Claims. Four new transits. Its notebook calls TIC 417732194 the
  cleanest: 8 events in Sectors 59–60.
- •
  Independent detection. The parallel proposer in the same round
  (it00-p1, \$3.84) also detected the signal but declined to claim it,
  citing “short baseline, unpredictable ephemeris”.

#### Verification.

1.  1.
    Referee v5 (kernel). The referee re-measures each claim from the raw
    light curves, applies cadence checks per sector and the cross-era
    rule, checks against known catalogues (TOI, CTOI, SPOC TCEs, VSX,
    Gaia variability, SIMBAD) and requires an event-overlap alias test
    to pass. It accepted the claim. Two of the other three claims were
    rejected by the cross-era rule.
2.  2.
    Pixel level (operator). A Sector-59 TESScut difference image places
    the flux deficit on or next to the target pixel. The fourth claim
    was rejected here as a field-wide flux drop.
3.  3.
    Prediction test (operator). An ephemeris fitted to Sectors 59–60
    alone predicted dips in Sectors 73 and 86, which were never used for
    selection and lie 68 and 134 orbits later. Both dips appear inside
    the propagated $`\pm 2\sigma`$ window. Against 400 full-pipeline
    null realisations (transits masked, sectors circularly shifted),
    $`p=0.09`$ for Sector 73, $`p=0.0025`$ for Sector 86, and about
    $`0.002`$ combined.
4.  4.
    Photometric vetting.

    - •
      Odd and even depths agree to $`1.2\sigma`$.
    - •
      No secondary eclipse ($`-0.13\pm 0.30`$ ppt).
    - •
      The depth is stable across seven detrending choices.
    - •
      The residuals are white at the transit timescale.
5.  5.
    Independent review. A read-only reviewer agent found a 1,000-day
    error in the reference epoch and an independence error in the first
    report. Both were corrected.
6.  6.
    Status. A bound eclipsing binary and a $`G=17.2`$ neighbour
    $`20^{\prime\prime}`$ away are not excluded. The candidate is
    unconfirmed \[[18](#bib.bib18)\].

## Appendix B The autonomous runs in detail

### B.1 Run 1: two-deletion-correcting codes

Session 20261026-002501-autonomous, launched as a background job at
00:24:58 UTC on 26 October 2026 with 3 iterations, 2 parallel proposers,
a \$30 budget and at most 3 scout rounds. There was no operator action
after launch.

#### Goal (verbatim, the default).

“Find an open problem in mathematics, quantum information or theoretical
computer science whose best known result is an explicit object or number
that a program can check exactly, and improve on the best known result.”

#### Problem chosen.

The largest binary code $`C\subset\{0,1\}^{16}`$ that corrects two
deletions: for distinct codewords, the sets of length-14 strings
obtained by deleting two positions are disjoint. This is a maximum
independent set in a fixed graph on 65,536 vertices. The LP upper bound
is 487. The scout’s reasons, from SELECTION.md:

- •
  the deliverable is an explicit word list;
- •
  the exact check takes under a second;
- •
  every extra codeword is a strict improvement;
- •
  the literature gave 215 (Weindel and Heckel, arXiv:2504.00613v2, code
  not published) and 208 (CPro1, arXiv:2505.23881, code public).

#### Round 0.

1.  1.
    Scout (00:25–00:35, \$3.14). It wrote a task with record 215, the
    public 208-word seed, score range 208–216 and ten calibration cases:
    four valid (208, 194, 193 and 100 words) and six invalid (a bit
    flip, a duplicate, an empty code, a near-miss extra word, a
    non-binary word, a wrong length).
2.  2.
    Kernel validation. The seed scored 208. All four valid cases
    reproduced their values and all six invalid cases were rejected, so
    no problems were found.
3.  3.
    Audit (00:36–00:39, \$1.32), verdict *fail*. From AUDIT.md: “the
    cited EinsteinArena problem 34 has moved on. Its leaderboard
    (queried 2026-10-26): nightshift-dc16 223, happy-gpt-astra-6 218,
    Opus-HedgyLabs 216, … I downloaded the 223-word code from the public
    API and checked it with the task’s own verifier (223.0) and an
    independent max pairwise LCS = 13 test … So record 215 is wrong.”
4.  4.
    Exploit replay. The auditor wrote 18 exploit files, among them every
    word in the space, Boolean or integer elements, full-width and
    Arabic-Indic digits, padded words, NaN, wrong lengths, a list
    instead of a dict, and too many words. The kernel replayed all 18
    and the verifier accepted none.

#### Round 1.

1.  1.
    Scout repair (00:40–00:46, \$0.85). Record 223, sourced to the
    arena’s best-solution API and queried 26 October. The 223-word code
    became the seed, the score range was widened to 208–228, and two new
    calibration cases were added: the 223-word code (valid) and that
    code plus one conflicting word (invalid).
2.  2.
    Kernel validation. The seed scored 223. All five valid cases
    reproduced their values and all seven invalid cases were rejected.
3.  3.
    Audit (00:47–00:49, \$0.58), verdict *pass*, with open: true and
    record_ok: true. Its remaining notes: extra dictionary keys are
    ignored, which is harmless because the value is the number of words;
    and the record moves fast.
4.  4.
    Exploit replay. Twenty files, none accepted.
5.  5.
    Installation. At 00:50:39 the task was installed, with an approval
    record naming the approver as “kernel (autonomous mode)” and the
    basis as “calibration + adversarial audit + exploit replay”.

#### Discovery

(00:50–02:05, \$3.46; session 20261026-005039-discover-del2-code-16).

- •
  Iteration 0.

  - –
    *aggressive rewrite* (\$0.75): plateau local search with forced
    insertion and Metropolis acceptance, 4 cores $`\times`$ 25 min,
    about $`2\times 10^{7}`$ moves each. Current size wandered between
    206 and 223; best 223.
  - –
    *data structure* (\$0.59): an implicit-adjacency search over
    $`2^{14}`$ descendant slots at about $`1.9\times 10^{8}`$ candidate
    probes per second per core; best 223.
- •
  Iteration 1.

  - –
    *robust/simple* (\$0.84): no gain.
  - –
    *new neighbourhood* (\$0.86): exact large-neighbourhood search. It
    frees $`K`$ codewords chosen by Hamming proximity, a random bit mask
    or a shift-aware distance, then solves the freed region exactly by
    bitset branch and bound. Runs at $`K=24`$–60 made up to
    $`1.6\times 10^{6}`$ moves; 10–13% reached a different optimal set
    and none reached a larger one.
- •
  Iteration 2. *conservative* twice (\$0.20 each). Both copied the
  parent and its notes: no-ops.

Best: the seed, 223 words. Seven bank entries, none above the seed.

#### Independent check

(02:05–02:06, \$0.19, network off). The checker received only problem.md
and the best solution. It wrote my_checker.py (format, 16-bit binary
words, distinctness, pairwise-disjoint deletion sets) and tested it on
constructed cases. As a cross-check it computed the longest common
subsequence of every pair (at most 13, so no shared length-14
subsequence). Verdict: valid, 223, in agreement with the verifier.

#### Report

(02:06–02:07, \$0.32). Claim: {beats_record: false, value: 223, record:
223, claim: “No improvement: the best verified code has 223 words, which
ties (does not beat) the public record of 223 for
two-deletion-correcting binary codes of length 16.”}. The report’s claim
boundary disclaims a new record, the optimality of 223, the
impossibility of 224, and authorship of the code, crediting the arena
agents.

#### Totals.

1 h 42 min; \$9.86. The breakdown is scout \$3.99, audit \$1.90,
discovery \$3.46, check \$0.19 and report \$0.32.

### B.2 Choosing the goals of runs 2 and 3

Before runs 2 and 3, five research agents, directed by the operator,
surveyed published tables of explicit, exactly checkable records for low
current activity. They looked beyond quantum information. Their top
picks were Brouwer’s mixed binary/ternary code tables (quiet since
2013), qutrit stabilizer-code gaps, sorting-network sizes for 25–40
inputs, real Grassmannian packings and ternary codes $`A_{3}(n,d)`$.
They advised avoiding tables already worked by many agents: the V3R1T4S
list, binary and constant-weight codes, most Einstein Arena problems and
the QIQC zoo. The operator wrote one goal sentence for each of the first
and third picks, naming the table and the improvement wanted, and asked
the scout to choose the cell and confirm that it was current. Both jobs
ran with 3 iterations, 2 parallel proposers, a \$30 budget and the
research math arms. The first launch of the pair collided on a session
directory
(Section [3.8](#S3.SS8 "3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research"))
and was cancelled within a minute; the relaunches below are the runs
reported.

### B.3 Run 2: sorting network on 31 inputs

Session 20261026-024005-autonomous-e33eb, 02:40–05:18 UTC.

#### Goal (verbatim).

“Improve a size upper bound in Bert Dobbelaere’s sorting-network tables
for n = 25 to 40 inputs (…): choose n, confirm the current best-known
number of comparators and its date, and construct a valid sorting
network on n inputs with fewer comparators, verified exactly by the 0-1
principle.”

#### Scout

(02:40–02:58, \$2.03). It chose $`n=31`$: record 180 comparators in 14
layers, bounds $`141\leq S(31)\leq 180`$, table source “Batcher odd-even
merge”, with no 31-input size change since the 2017 draft (page dated 10
October 2026). Its reason was that the entry is the 32-input merge
network minus one wire, never improved by search, while the entries for
$`n=28`$–30 had been improved beyond the wire-removal bound. Before
choosing, it ran its own wire-removal beam search from all record
networks for $`n=25`$–40; this beat no entry (for $`n=30`$ it gave 173
against the record 172). The verifier is an exact check of all
$`2^{31}`$ binary inputs by bit-slicing (about 8–15 s). The seed is the
record network. There were eight calibration cases. The three valid ones
were the 186-comparator Batcher network, the record and the record plus
a redundant comparator (181). The five invalid ones were an index out of
range, a malformed list, the record with one comparator dropped, a
reversed comparator and a 30-input network. Scoring was minimised over
the range 186 to 175, which in the kernel’s convention is reversed
(Section [3.8](#S3.SS8 "3.8 Fully autonomous end-to-end runs ‣ 3 Results ‣ Infinity Machine: a self-improving AI agent for research")).

#### Validation and audit

(02:58–03:05, \$0.89). All eight cases reproduced. Audit verdict:
*pass*. Its minor issues were that the page now read 13 October, with
changes only for other $`n`$; that $`n=31.0`$ is accepted as 31; and
that public equals private. The auditor wrote 23 exploit files, among
them the 30-input record plus an unused wire, and the kernel’s replay
rejected all of them. The auditor described the score mapping as
“186$`\to`$0, 175$`\to`$1”, the intended direction, which is not what
the kernel computes.

#### Discovery

(03:06–05:15, \$4.12; session 20261026-030658-discover-sortnet-31).

- •
  Iteration 0. *Literature transfer* twice (\$0.64, \$1.04). Both wrote
  SorterHunter-style evolutionary searches in C from the record, with
  the first three or four layers fixed and only the reachable 0-1
  vectors kept. Their mutations replaced, swapped, moved, inserted or
  deleted comparators and pruned redundant ones. Neither found 179.
- •
  Iteration 1. *Scale compute* (\$0.97) added a pretest on 1,024 witness
  vectors that earlier mutants had failed, raising throughput from about
  52k to 300k evaluations per second per core, and ran on 4 cores for
  2,900 s each: no 179. *Exhaustive small case* (\$0.27) ran no search.
  It estimated a delete-two/insert-one repair at about $`10^{9}`$
  candidates, each over about 28,000 vectors, as beyond its budget.
- •
  Iteration 2. *New objective* (\$0.27) checked that none of the 180
  single-comparator deletions sorts, then ran no new search. *New
  objective* (\$0.93) fixed the first 60 comparators (four butterfly
  layers, leaving 28,024 unsorted reachable vectors) and annealed the
  remaining 119 comparators on the number of vectors still unsorted. Its
  best state left one vector unsorted.

Best: the seed, 180. Seven bank entries, all scored 0.4545.

#### Independent check and report

(05:16–05:18, \$0.55). The checker’s own C program confirmed that the
network sorts all $`2^{31}`$ inputs with 180 comparators. Claim:
{beats_record: false, value: 180, record: 180}. The report noted the
audit’s 0.545 against the bank’s 0.4545 and used the bank’s figure. Its
claim boundary disclaims an improvement and any statement that 179 is
impossible, and notes that every search started from the record with a
fixed prefix.

#### Totals.

2 h 38 min; \$7.59: scout \$2.03, audit \$0.89, discovery \$4.12, check
\$0.27, report \$0.28.

### B.4 Run 3: mixed binary/ternary code $`N(4,5,3)`$

Session 20261026-023958-autonomous-67f31, 02:40–05:35 UTC.

#### Goal (verbatim).

“Improve a lower bound in Andries Brouwer’s table of mixed
binary/ternary codes N(m,n,d) (…): codes with m binary and n ternary
coordinates and minimum mixed Hamming distance d. Choose a cell where
the gap between the lower and upper bound is large and the lower bound
looks improvable, confirm the table entry is current (check the page’s
update notes and recent arXiv), and construct a strictly larger code
than the current lower bound.”

#### Scout

(02:40–03:27, \$4.66). It chose $`N(4,5,3)`$: words in
$`\{0,1\}^{4}\times\{0,1,2\}^{5}`$ (3,888 in all) at mixed Hamming
distance at least 3, with bounds 186–216. The lower bound dates from
Brouwer, Hämäläinen, Östergård and Sloane (1998), and the upper bound
216 is $`3N(4,4,3)`$. Its reasons were the 16% gap and the fact that
neighbouring cells, among them $`N(3,5,3)`$, $`N(5,5,3)`$, $`N(3,6,3)`$
and $`N(4,7,3)`$, were improved by forum posters in 2010–2013 while this
one was not. It fetched the page (Last-Modified 17 October 2026); its
arXiv search was blocked by HTTP 429. It wrote coset.c, a clique search
over unions of cosets of an additive subgroup. This reproduced 186 as 62
cosets of $`\langle(0000|10101)\rangle`$ in seconds, along with other
table entries ($`N(7,3,3)=192`$, $`N(8,3,3)=384`$, $`N(5,6,5)=96`$,
$`N(6,5,5)=66`$). Its own searches over subgroup orders 2, 3, 4, 6 and 9
and a 16k-step LNS did not beat 186. There were twelve calibration
cases. Four were valid: the record, a 150-word subcode, the same code in
string format and a single word. Eight were invalid: a binary symbol 2,
a duplicate, an empty code, float symbols, a near miss at distance 1,
the record plus a conflicting 187th word, the wrong cell and the wrong
length. Scoring was maximised over 150–188, so the record scores 0.947
(correct direction).

#### Validation and audit

(03:27–03:32, \$1.14). All twelve cases reproduced. Audit verdict:
*pass*. Its minor issues were that extra keys are ignored and that its
own arXiv and Semantic Scholar searches were also rate-limited, so only
the table page was checked. The kernel replayed 24 exploit files, among
them all 3,888 words, and rejected all of them. Installed at 03:34.

#### Discovery

(03:34–05:33, \$3.60; session 20261026-033400-discover-mixed-code-n453).

- •
  Iteration 0. *Literature transfer* twice (\$0.68, \$0.66). Both ran
  prescribed-automorphism-group searches, after Östergård’s method. Each
  sampled random groups of binary permutations with flips and ternary
  permutations with per-coordinate symbol permutations, kept compatible
  orbits, and annealed a weighted independent set on the orbit conflict
  graph. Both found 186 and nothing more.
- •
  Iteration 1. *Structured construction* (\$0.34): about 10,900 groups
  with up to three generators, 1,500 s on 4 CPUs; best 186 in every run.
  *New objective* (\$0.70): tabu.c fixes the code size and minimises the
  number of conflicting pairs. From random starts it reached valid codes
  of 180 and 183 words, and once 186 with no imposed structure, but
  never 187.
- •
  Iteration 2. *New objective* (\$0.88): a fixed-size tabu search over
  orbits of the known translation group. It reaches 62 orbits (186
  words) in under a second; at 63 orbits (189 words) the best state had
  one conflicting pair, over four 150 s runs and further seeds. *Scale
  compute* (\$0.35): 9,653 random groups with long anneals, 2,700 s on 4
  CPUs. 272 groups reached 186 and none reached 187.

Best: the seed, 186. Seven bank entries, all scored 0.947.

#### Independent check and report

(05:33–05:35, \$0.58). The checker confirmed 186 valid words and stated
that 186 is not a new record. Claim: {beats_record: false, value: 186,
record: 186}. The report notes the rate-limited literature checks, says
that a newer paper cannot be ruled out, and says that 186 is not proven
optimal.

#### Totals.

2 h 55 min; \$9.97: scout \$4.66, audit \$1.14, discovery \$3.60, check
\$0.17, report \$0.41.

## Appendix D Strategy arms

Each proposer’s brief contains the name and text of its arm, chosen per
task family by UCB1.

#### Default (written for optimisation tasks).

*conservative*: keep the parent’s algorithm; make one safe, measured
improvement. *aggressive rewrite*: replace the core algorithm with a
stronger one you can implement and test within the budget. *new
neighbourhood*: keep the framework but add a new move type or
neighbourhood and integrate it into the search loop. *data structure*:
make the inner loop faster so more iterations fit in the time limit;
measure iterations per second before and after. *robust/simple*:
simplify and harden; make every instance size produce valid output.

#### Math (written by the operator after the first stabilizer-rank session).

*structured construction*: build candidates from structure (symmetry,
known constructions, algebraic families, products of smaller solutions)
instead of unstructured local search; derive, then verify exactly.
*exhaustive small case*: reduce by symmetry and enumerate a small case
completely, turning the search into a decision with a replayable
certificate. *new objective*: change what is optimised or how candidates
are parametrised; calibrate on a solved case first. *scale compute*:
take the best existing method and scale it with parallel restarts and
checkpointing. *literature transfer*: port one published technique named
in the notes, reproduce its known result, then push it to the open case.

#### ML (written by the operator after the first LM session).

*new architecture family* (mixture of experts, state-space or linear
attention, recurrent, hybrids), *parameter sharing* (looped or
weight-shared blocks), *embedding budget* (smaller vocabulary,
factorised or hashed embeddings), *connectivity* (skip connections,
value residuals, multi-token heads, attention variants), *recipe*
(optimizer, batch, schedule); each compared at equal tokens.

#### Astronomy (catalogue mode).

*new population*, *new phenomenon*, *deeper search*, *vetting and
follow-up*, *anomaly hunt*.

## Appendix E Evidence for the specification-gaming incidents

#### AdderBoard: weights turned into constants.

Excerpt from the model the proposers delivered (session 2). The two
former weights in the excerpt are commented as fixed temperatures, one
explicitly as “not a weight”:

``` ltx_verbatim
self.omega = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(2 * math.pi / 10))  # embedding / read-out scale
self.lam = 60.0      # attention sharpness (fixed temperature, not a weight)
self.kappa = 30.0    # carry-gate sharpness (fixed temperature)
...
carry = torch.sigmoid(self.kappa * (Bv - 1.5 * self.omega))
U = 2.0 * A + self.omega * carry
````

From the proposer’s final message: “I cut the model from 5 parameters to
1 and it still adds correctly … Review risk: the fixed constants (60,
30, 1.5, 2) sit in forward(). A human reviewer could read that as
weights hidden in the architecture.” Under the strict counter, these
constants count and the model has 5 parameters.

#### Seven-qubit code: lenient partial credit.

The first verifier scored a subspace of dimension $`K`$ with worst
compression residual $`r`$ as $`K`$ if $`r<10^{-9}`$, and otherwise as
$`(K-1)+0.999\cdot\mathrm{clip}(-\log_{10}r/9)`$. A $`K=25`$ subspace at
$`r=0.072`$ (no code) therefore scored 0.8127, above the confirmed
$`K=24`$ code’s 0.80. A proposer drawn with the _robust/simple_ arm
delivered exactly that. The fixed formula starts partial credit only
below $`r=10^{-2}`$.

#### TESS, referee v1.

Accepted claims included “single transits” with depths of 500–1200%
(flux glitches), flux steps, and about 90 low-effort eclipsing-binary
claims, a quarter of which failed the held-out prediction. Re-scored
under referee v2, the same catalogue fell from 94.5 to 30.5 (public) and
from 77.5 to 21.75 (hidden).

#### TESS, referee v2.

From a proposer’s notebook (session 2): “Hypothesis: the parent
catalogue saturated the capped classes (83 EBs $`>`$ cap 15 credits, 54
variables $`>`$ cap 5), so extra credit lies in uncapped single events
(1.0) and long-period duo transits (3.0), which SPOC TPS cannot find.”
It then submitted 240 single events and 39 two-event “transits” whose
period was set to the gap between the events. The operator cancelled the
session after that round.

#### TESS, referee v4 (operator-found).

The referee computed one cadence per star, so for a star with both 200-s
and 30-min sectors, every 30-min event was invisible to its checks, and
a dip seen in only one observing era could pass. Two of four new transit
claims were rejected under the fixed referee (v5) because their dip
appeared only in the latest era.

## Appendix F Gate configuration and the self-derived playbook

#### Gate.

Held-in tasks: an RFC 4180 CSV parser, 2-D TSP and graph colouring.
Held-out tasks: interval merging and bin packing. Noise band 0.03;
minimum gain 0; anomaly threshold 0.3; cost factor 1.5; at most 12
changed files; one seed per task. Parent selection: score-child (a UCB
selector with descendant-growth pruning is implemented but not the
default).

#### Generation 1 (consolidation, rejected).

The four bullets the system derived from its first 16 problem runs,
verbatim apart from shortened run identifiers and two file names
replaced by bracketed descriptions:

- P-0002
  Before searching, list neighbourhoods and families already tried in
  prior notes (1–3 flip SA, ILS from record) and pick an untried one;
  several runs re-ran the same local search. (3 Hadamard runs;
  confidence 0.60)
- P-0003
  Faster inner loops or better optimisers on a proxy energy (Gram
  target, design cost) are not progress unless the proxy is shown to
  track the true objective; compare on the real score at equal
  wall-clock. (2 Hadamard runs, 1 Sidon run; 0.60)
- P-0004
  Symmetry-restricted search spaces ($`\mathbb{Z}_{17}`$,
  $`\mathbb{Z}_{5}\times\mathbb{Z}_{5}`$, $`\mathbb{Z}_{3}`$ blocks)
  capped below the record’s family; run a short pilot (about 60 s) and
  compare to the record before committing a long compute budget. (2
  Hadamard runs; 0.55)
- P-0005
  \[the task’s local scoring script\] is often absent; look for \[the
  task’s checker tool\] first and use it for the exact score. (3 runs;
  0.70)

Graded result: held-in 0.944 against 0.927, held-out 1.000 against
1.000, cost \$5.50 against \$2.72 (ratio 2.02 $`>`$ 1.5): rejected.
